items.q: The PC on this port is hard-set to 100 Mbps full duplex. What's wrong?
o: A duplex mismatch: the switch has fallen back to half duplex
A faulty cable causing CRC errors
The port has been shut down

sets.title: The CompTIA troubleshooting methodology
sets.intro: Put the seven steps in order.
items: Establish a theory of probable cause
Test the theory to determine the cause
Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem and identify potential effects
Implement the solution or escalate as necessary
Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures if applicable
Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned
sets.e: If testing doesn't confirm the theory, go back and establish a new one, or escalate.

items: Discover: the client broadcasts to find a DHCP server

Acknowledge: the server confirms the lease
sets.e: Clients start renewing at 50% of the lease time.

coverage.title: Where your notes and the official objectives differ
coverage.intro: Module 1's lessons are numbered one ahead of CompTIA's objectives, because the course starts with an overview lesson. This quiz uses the official numbering:
coverage.watchTitle: Things in the notes to watch for in the exam:
watch: The notes call Cat 7 'SCTP' and describe the Stream Control Transmission Protocol. The cable term is ScTP, screened twisted pair. They're unrelated.
The notes list channels 1, 6, 11 and 14 as non-overlapping. Channel 14 is Japan-only and 802.11b-only, so the exam answer is 1, 6 and 11.
The notes say all SNMP versions use community strings. Only v1 and v2c do; SNMPv3 uses usernames with proper authentication and encryption.
The notes call it a full mesh. Every leaf connects to every spine, but leaves don't connect to each other and spines don't either, so some sources call it a partial mesh.
The exam expects the CompTIA steps in order: identify, theory, test, plan and implement (or escalate), verify and prevent, document.

1.8: Covers SDN, SD-WAN, VXLAN, zero trust, SASE/SSE, IaC, IPv6, dual stack and tunnelling. NAT64 isn't covered, so two extra questions are added on it.

questions.q: Which OSI layer adds MAC addresses and builds frames?
questions.e: The Data Link layer frames Layer 3 packets and adds source and destination MAC addresses, plus a trailer with a CRC.

questions.q: At which OSI layer do routers make forwarding decisions?
questions.e: Routers forward packets using logical (IP) addresses, which belong to Layer 3.

questions.q: What is the PDU called at the Transport layer when TCP is used?
questions.e: TCP data at Layer 4 is a segment (UDP's is a datagram). Layer 3 is a packet, Layer 2 a frame and Layer 1 bits.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles data formatting, encryption and compression, such as converting between character sets?
questions.e: The Presentation layer makes sure both sides agree on how data is represented: formats, encryption and compression.

questions.q: Which layer is responsible for setting up, managing and tearing down sessions between applications?
questions.e: The Session layer keeps separate conversations separate and controls when they start and end.

questions.q: A technician finds a damaged patch cable. Which OSI layer is the problem at?
questions.e: Cables, connectors, signals and NICs' electrical side are all Layer 1, the Physical layer.

questions.q: Which list puts the OSI layers in order from Layer 1 to Layer 7?
o: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
Physical, Network, Data Link, Transport, Session, Application, Presentation
Data Link, Physical, Network, Transport, Presentation, Session, Application
Physical, Data Link, Transport, Network, Session, Presentation, Application
questions.e: A memory aid from Layer 1 up: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.

questions.q: What happens to data as it moves down the OSI layers on the sending device?
o: Each layer adds its own header (encapsulation)
The data is encrypted at every layer
questions.e: Encapsulation wraps data in headers on the way down. The receiver de-encapsulates on the way up.

questions.q: Which OSI layer is a switch mainly associated with?
questions.e: A standard switch forwards frames using MAC addresses, so it's a Layer 2 device. A multilayer switch can also route at Layer 3.

questions.q: Which devices work purely at Layer 1?
questions.e: Layer 1 devices just pass on electrical or light signals without reading any addresses.

questions.q: Which Layer 2 sublayer adds the physical (hardware) addresses to a frame?
questions.e: Layer 2 has two sublayers: LLC describes the Layer 3 payload and MAC handles hardware addressing and media access.

questions.q: A frame fails its CRC check when it arrives at a switch. What happens to it?
o: It is discarded, and upper layers (such as TCP) must resend the data
It is repaired by the switch
It is forwarded with a warning
It is sent back to the sender at Layer 2
questions.e: Layer 2 detects errors with the frame check sequence but doesn't correct them. Bad frames are dropped.

questions.q: Which OSI layer do HTTP, DNS and SMTP belong to?
questions.e: These are application protocols that programs use to request network services.

questions.q: Which OSI layer adds source and destination port numbers?
questions.e: TCP and UDP headers carry the port numbers that identify which application the data belongs to.

questions.q: Users can ping a server by IP address but can't open its website. Pings prove the path works up to which layer at least?
questions.e: A successful ping (ICMP) shows Layers 1 to 3 are working. The fault is likely higher up, such as the web service, a port or DNS.

questions.q: Which statement about the TCP/IP (DoD) model is correct?
o: It has four layers, with Application covering OSI Layers 5 to 7
It has seven layers like OSI
It replaces IP addresses with MAC addresses
questions.e: The DoD/TCP-IP model groups OSI layers: Application (5-7), Host-to-Host/Transport (4), Internet (3) and Network Access (1-2).

questions.q: What is the PDU called at Layer 3?
questions.e: Data at the Network layer is a packet, carrying source and destination IP addresses.

questions.q: Which item works at the Physical layer?
questions.e: Frequencies, voltages, connectors and cable types are all Layer 1 details.

questions.q: What is the key difference between an IDS and an IPS?
o: An IDS detects and alerts, while an IPS sits inline and can block traffic
An IDS blocks traffic, while an IPS only logs it
An IPS only works on wireless networks
questions.e: An IDS passively watches a copy of traffic. An IPS is inline, so it can stop attacks but may also block legitimate traffic (false positives).

questions.q: A website has three web servers. Which device spreads incoming requests across them?
questions.e: Load balancers share traffic between servers and stop sending to any that fail health checks.

questions.q: What does a forward proxy server do?
o: Makes requests to the internet on behalf of clients, and can cache and filter content
questions.e: Proxies fetch content for clients, cache it for others and can enforce web filtering.

questions.q: What is the main difference between NAS and a SAN?
o: NAS shares files over the network; a SAN gives servers block-level storage that appears local
NAS is faster than any SAN
A SAN only works over Wi-Fi
questions.e: NAS uses file protocols like SMB or NFS. SANs use Fibre Channel or iSCSI to present block storage.

questions.q: A company has 60 access points that need consistent settings and firmware. What should they use?
o: A range extender on every floor
questions.e: A WLC centrally manages lightweight access points: configuration, firmware, channels and roaming.

questions.q: What does a content delivery network (CDN) do?
o: Serves web content from servers close to users, around the world
Encrypts all traffic on a LAN
questions.e: CDNs cache content in many locations to cut latency for geographically spread users.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the TTL field in an IP packet?
o: It limits how many routers the packet can pass through, so it can't loop forever
questions.e: Each router decrements TTL by one. At zero the packet is discarded, usually with an ICMP 'time exceeded' message.

questions.q: Video calls are choppy when the network is busy. Which feature gives voice and video traffic priority?
questions.e: QoS prioritises time-sensitive traffic to reduce latency, jitter and packet loss during congestion.

questions.q: Which device protects a trusted network from an untrusted one using allow and deny rules?
questions.e: Firewall rules can match IP addresses, ports, protocols, direction and connection state.

questions.q: What is a virtual appliance?
o: Network functions such as a firewall or router running as software in a VM
A router with no power supply
questions.e: Many appliances are available as virtual versions, common in cloud and virtualised environments.

questions.q: What does a VPN do?
o: Creates an encrypted tunnel so traffic can cross an untrusted network securely
questions.e: VPNs encapsulate and usually encrypt traffic, hiding it inside other packets.

questions.q: What does a Wi-Fi range extender depend on?
o: An existing access point; it repeats that signal but can't create a WLAN itself
Nothing; it creates its own network
questions.e: Extenders repeat an AP's signal to reach further clients.

questions.q: Where is an IPS typically placed?
o: Inline, behind the firewall, so traffic passes through it
questions.e: Being inline is what lets an IPS drop malicious traffic as it passes.

questions.q: A layer 3 switch differs from a standard switch because it can also:
questions.e: Multilayer switches combine switching with routing, often used for inter-VLAN routing.

questions.q: Which device would you use to let internal users browse the web while blocking gambling sites and caching common pages?
o: A proxy server with content filtering
questions.e: Proxies can filter URLs and categories and cache content to save bandwidth.

questions.q: An IDS raises an alert for normal backup traffic every night. What is this?
questions.e: False positives are alerts on harmless traffic. False negatives are real attacks that go unnoticed.

questions.q: Which protocols commonly connect servers to a SAN?
questions.e: SANs carry block storage traffic using Fibre Channel or iSCSI (SCSI over IP).

questions.q: What does a router change when it forwards a packet to the next network?
o: The Layer 2 frame header, while keeping the source and destination IP the same
questions.e: Routers rebuild the frame for each hop with new MAC addresses. NAT is a separate function that changes IPs.

questions.q: What is a virtual private cloud (VPC)?
o: An isolated section of a public cloud where a customer defines their own IP ranges, subnets and routing
A cloud only one company in the world can use
questions.e: VPCs let customers build private networks inside a provider's shared infrastructure.

questions.q: Which cloud gateway lets instances in a private subnet reach the internet without being reachable from it?
questions.e: A NAT gateway allows outbound connections only. An internet gateway allows two-way traffic for resources with public IPs.

questions.q: A company needs a dedicated, private link from its data centre to its cloud provider rather than using the internet. What should it use?
questions.e: Direct Connect-style services give a private, consistent link through a provider partner.

questions.q: What are network security groups (NSGs) in the cloud?
o: Firewall-style rules that allow or deny traffic to cloud resources
Groups of users with the same password
Physical racks in a data centre
questions.e: NSGs (Azure) and security groups (AWS) filter traffic to instances and interfaces.

questions.q: What is network functions virtualisation (NFV)?
o: Running network functions such as routing and firewalls as software instead of dedicated hardware
questions.e: NFV underpins cloud networking: each function is a virtual network function (VNF).

questions.q: Which cloud service model gives the customer virtual servers, storage and networking to build on?
questions.e: IaaS provides infrastructure. The customer manages the OS and above.

questions.q: In SaaS, who is responsible for maintaining the application?
questions.e: SaaS customers manage their users and data. The provider runs everything else.

questions.q: A business keeps sensitive data on its own private cloud but uses public cloud for its website. What model is this?
questions.e: Hybrid combines private and public clouds, often moving workloads between them.

questions.q: Adding more identical servers to share the load is called:
questions.e: Vertical scaling adds resources to one instance. Horizontal adds more instances.

questions.q: What is elasticity in cloud computing?
o: Resources expand and shrink automatically with demand
Data that can be stretched across disks
questions.e: Elasticity is automatic scaling in near real time, so you only pay for what you use.

questions.q: What is multitenancy?
o: Many customers sharing the same infrastructure while being kept logically separate
questions.e: Tenants share hardware but can't see each other's data.

questions.q: Which cloud model is shared by several organisations with the same requirements, such as local councils?
questions.e: Community clouds serve a group with shared concerns such as compliance.

questions.q: Which is a common way for a small office to connect securely to its cloud network over the internet?
questions.e: Site-to-site VPNs link an office router to the cloud provider's VPN gateway.

questions.q: A developer wants to deploy code without managing servers or the operating system. Which model fits?
questions.e: PaaS gives a ready platform, with the OS and runtime managed by the provider.

questions.q: Network security lists in the cloud are most like which traditional feature?
o: Access control lists applied to subnets
questions.e: Security lists act as subnet-level ACLs in a virtual cloud network.

questions.q: What does an internet gateway do in a VPC?
o: Allows two-way traffic between the internet and resources with public IPs
questions.e: Internet gateways route traffic in and out of public subnets.

questions.q: Increasing the RAM and CPU of an existing cloud server is:
questions.e: Scaling up (vertical) makes one instance bigger.

questions.q: Why is NFV important to cloud providers?
o: It lets them deliver routers, firewalls and load balancers to customers as software on shared hardware
It removes the need for any hardware
questions.e: Virtual network functions can be created and chained on demand for each customer.

questions.q: Which port does SSH use?
questions.e: SSH (and SFTP) use TCP 22. Telnet uses 23 and is unencrypted.

questions.q: Which ports does DHCP use?
questions.e: DHCP servers listen on UDP 67 and clients use UDP 68.

questions.q: Which port does DNS use?
questions.e: DNS uses UDP 53 for most queries and TCP 53 for zone transfers and large responses.

questions.q: Which ports does SNMP use?
o: UDP 161 for polling and 162 for traps
questions.e: Managers poll agents on 161. Agents send traps to the manager on 162.

questions.q: Which port does syslog use by default?
questions.e: Syslog sends log messages to a central server on UDP 514.

questions.q: Which port does NTP use?
questions.e: NTP synchronises clocks over UDP 123.

questions.q: Which port is used by LDAPS?
questions.e: LDAP uses 389 and LDAP over TLS (LDAPS) uses 636.

questions.q: Which port does Microsoft SQL Server use by default?
questions.e: SQL Server listens on TCP 1433.

questions.q: Which ports are used by SIP?
questions.e: SIP sets up VoIP and video calls on 5060 (unencrypted) and 5061 (TLS).

questions.q: Which port does TFTP use?
questions.e: TFTP is a simple file transfer with no authentication, often used to load device configs and firmware.

questions.q: Which port is used by SMB file sharing?
questions.e: Modern SMB runs directly over TCP 445.

questions.q: Which port does SMTPS use in the Network+ objectives?
questions.e: CompTIA lists SMTPS as 587 (secure mail submission). Port 25 is plain SMTP between servers.

questions.q: How does a TCP connection start?
o: A three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
questions.e: The handshake sets up sequence numbers before data flows. FINs close the connection.

questions.q: Why is UDP used for VoIP and streaming?
o: It has low overhead and no retransmissions, so it's faster
questions.e: For real-time traffic, resending late packets is pointless, so connectionless UDP suits it.

questions.q: Which protocol does ping use?
questions.e: Ping sends ICMP echo requests and waits for echo replies.

questions.q: Which protocol resolves an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local network?
questions.e: ARP broadcasts to ask who has an IP, and the owner replies with its MAC address.

questions.q: Which protocol creates simple tunnels that can carry many protocol types but doesn't encrypt them by itself?
questions.e: GRE encapsulates packets in a tunnel, often combined with IPsec for encryption.

questions.q: Which IPsec protocol provides encryption of the payload?
questions.e: ESP encrypts and authenticates. AH authenticates only. IKE negotiates the keys and security associations.

questions.q: Which part of IPsec negotiates keys and sets up the secure connection?
questions.e: Internet Key Exchange handles negotiation and key exchange before data is protected.

questions.q: Which traffic type sends one packet to all hosts on the local subnet?
questions.e: Broadcasts reach every host in the broadcast domain. Routers don't forward them.

questions.q: Which traffic type sends to a group of subscribed hosts, such as for streaming video to many viewers?
questions.e: Multicast delivers one stream to hosts that have joined the group.

questions.q: Which traffic type sends to the nearest of several servers sharing the same address, as used by DNS root servers?
questions.e: With anycast, routing delivers the packet to the closest instance of the shared address.

questions.q: A web server must be reachable for both HTTP and HTTPS. Which ports should the firewall allow?
questions.e: HTTP uses 80 and HTTPS uses 443.

questions.q: Which port does RDP use?
questions.e: RDP gives GUI remote control of Windows on TCP 3389.

questions.q: Which LDAP port is unencrypted?
questions.e: LDAPS (636) adds TLS encryption.

questions.q: Which protocol is used by hosts to join multicast groups?
questions.e: IGMP lets hosts tell routers which multicast groups they want.

questions.q: What is the maximum recommended length of a UTP Ethernet run?
questions.e: The 100 m limit includes patch leads. Longer runs need a switch or fibre.

questions.q: Which fibre type uses a laser and a very thin core to carry signals over long distances?
questions.e: Single-mode's 8 to 10 micron core carries one light path, reaching many kilometres.

questions.q: Which fibre type has a wider core, uses LED or VCSEL light, and is used for shorter runs within buildings?
questions.e: Multimode (50 or 62.5 micron core) suits LANs and data centres over shorter distances.

questions.q: Cable running above a suspended ceiling used for air circulation should be:
questions.e: Plenum cable gives off less toxic smoke if it burns, which matters in air-handling spaces.

questions.q: Which small form factor fibre connector, about half the size of SC, has a latch and is the most common on SFP modules?
questions.e: LC (Lucent Connector) is small form factor and the most common on modern transceivers.

questions.q: Which fibre connector carries many fibres in one ferrule, used for 40 and 100 Gbps links?
questions.e: Multi-fibre Push On (MPO) connectors bundle 12 or more fibres.

questions.q: Which fibre connector uses a bayonet twist-lock?
questions.e: ST (straight tip) twists to lock. SC is square push-pull.

questions.q: Which connector is screwed onto coaxial cable for cable modems and TV?
questions.e: F-type connectors are used with RG-6 coax.

questions.q: What is a DAC cable?
o: A short copper twinax cable with transceivers fixed on each end, used between nearby switches and servers
questions.e: Direct attach copper is a cheap alternative to fibre for very short, high-speed links.

questions.q: What is the difference between SFP and QSFP transceivers?
o: QSFP is a quad version carrying four lanes for higher speeds such as 40 or 100 Gbps
questions.e: SFP/SFP+ handle a single lane (1 or 10 Gbps). QSFP variants carry four lanes.

questions.q: Which cable category is the minimum for 10 Gbps Ethernet over a full 100 metres?
questions.e: Cat 6 only manages 10 Gbps to about 55 metres. Cat 6a supports it to 100 metres.

questions.q: Which cable category supports 25 or 40 Gbps over short distances of about 30 metres?
questions.e: Cat 8 is designed for data centre links up to around 30 metres.

questions.q: When is STP better than UTP?
o: In areas with high electrical interference, such as near motors or machinery
When you want the cheapest cable
questions.e: Shielding reduces EMI but STP is thicker, dearer and must be grounded.

questions.q: Which IEEE standard family covers Ethernet?
questions.e: 802.3 is Ethernet. 802.11 is Wi-Fi and 802.1Q is VLAN tagging.

questions.q: Which wireless WAN option suits a remote farm with no wired broadband, though it has high latency?
questions.e: Satellite reaches remote areas. Geostationary satellites add significant latency; low-orbit services reduce it.

questions.q: Why do fibre links usually need two strands?
o: One strand transmits and the other receives
questions.e: Most fibre links use a Tx and an Rx strand. Some transceivers (bidirectional) use one strand with two wavelengths.

questions.q: Which connector is used for telephone lines?
questions.e: RJ11 is smaller than RJ45 and used for phone lines and DSL.

questions.q: Which coaxial connector uses a quick twist-and-lock design, common on older CCTV and test equipment?
questions.e: BNC connectors lock with a quarter turn.

questions.q: A switch has an empty SFP+ port and you need to connect single-mode fibre. What do you need?
o: A single-mode SFP+ transceiver that matches the fibre and the switch
questions.e: The port, transceiver and cable must all match: speed, mode and wavelength.

questions.q: Which device converts fibre to twisted pair copper as a standalone box?
questions.e: Media converters join two cable types, most commonly fibre to Cat cable.

questions.q: What does cellular 5G offer for networks?
o: High-speed wireless WAN connectivity, often used as a backup or for remote sites
questions.e: Cellular links can provide primary or failover WAN connections.

questions.q: Which statement about coaxial cable types is correct?
o: RG-6 is 75 ohm and used for cable TV and broadband
RG-6 is used for 10 Gbps Ethernet
Coax is only used in fibre networks
questions.e: RG-6 and RG-59 are 75 ohm. RG-8 and similar are 50 ohm for radio work.

questions.q: Which topology connects every device to a central switch, so one failed cable affects only that device?
questions.e: Star is the most common LAN topology. If the central device fails, everything goes down.

questions.q: Which topology gives the most redundancy, with every node connected to every other node?
questions.e: Full mesh is very resilient but expensive. Partial mesh is a compromise.

questions.q: In a three-tier network design, which layer do end users' PCs plug into?
questions.e: Access switches connect end devices and handle VLAN membership, PoE and port security.

questions.q: Which three-tier layer handles inter-VLAN routing, policy and aggregates access switches?
questions.e: Distribution sits between core and access, applying policy and aggregating traffic.

questions.q: What is a collapsed core?
o: A design where the distribution and core layers are combined
A design with no access layer
questions.e: Collapsed core is cheaper and simpler, suiting small and medium campuses, but less resilient.

questions.q: In a spine-and-leaf data centre, how are switches connected?
o: Every leaf switch connects to every spine switch
Leaf switches connect only to each other
Spine switches connect in a ring
Each server connects directly to a spine
questions.e: Each leaf has a link to every spine, so traffic between any two leaves crosses exactly one spine (leaf, spine, leaf).

questions.q: What is east-west traffic?
o: Traffic moving between servers inside the data centre
questions.e: North-south traffic enters or leaves the network. East-west stays inside, such as server to server.

questions.q: Why does spine-and-leaf suit modern data centres?
o: It handles heavy east-west traffic with predictable, low latency and scales by adding leaves
It removes the need for switches
It works only for small offices
questions.e: Equal-cost paths through the spines make performance predictable and easy to scale.

questions.q: A WAN link connects exactly two offices. What topology is this?
questions.e: Point-to-point links have only two endpoints.

questions.q: Users downloading files from the internet create which traffic flow?
questions.e: Traffic crossing the network edge, in or out, is north-south.

questions.q: A company network uses star topologies in each building, joined by point-to-point links. What is the overall topology?
questions.e: A mix of topologies is a hybrid.

questions.q: Which three-tier layer provides fast backbone switching between buildings or to the data centre?
questions.e: The core is built for speed and resilience, with minimal processing.

questions.q: What is a key weakness of a basic star topology?
o: The central device is a single point of failure
It needs every node connected to every other
questions.e: Redundant central devices (a mesh design) remove the single point of failure.

questions.q: Hub-and-spoke WAN designs send branch-to-branch traffic:
questions.e: Spokes connect to the hub, so branch traffic goes through it. Mesh designs allow direct links.

questions.q: Why is partial mesh often chosen over full mesh?
o: It gives redundancy for key links at a lower cost
questions.e: Full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links, which gets expensive quickly.

questions.q: Which of these is a private (RFC 1918) address?
A Windows PC shows the address 169.254.33.10. What does this tell you?
o: It couldn't reach a DHCP server and gave itself an APIPA address
It has a valid public address
It is using a loopback address
It is on a guest VLAN
questions.e: APIPA (169.254.0.0/16) is self-assigned when DHCP fails and only works on the local segment.

questions.q: What is the IPv4 loopback range?
questions.e: 127.0.0.1 is the usual loopback address, used to test the local TCP/IP stack.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses are in a /26 subnet?
questions.e: A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 addresses, minus the network and broadcast = 62.

questions.q: What is the subnet mask for /27?
questions.e: /27 means 27 ones: the last octet is 11100000 = 224.

questions.q: What is the broadcast address of 192.168.10.70/26?
questions.e: /26 blocks go up in 64s: 0, 64, 128. 70 sits in the 64 block, so the broadcast is 127.

questions.q: What is the network (subnet) ID for 10.1.1.200/27?
questions.e: /27 blocks go up in 32s: 192 to 223 contains 200, so the subnet ID is .192.

questions.q: Which subnet mask is best for a point-to-point WAN link that needs only two addresses?
questions.e: A /30 has 4 addresses: network, two usable hosts and broadcast. (/31 is also used on some routers.)

questions.q: A department needs 50 hosts. What is the smallest subnet that fits?
questions.e: /27 gives only 30 usable. /26 gives 62.

questions.q: Which address class has a first octet from 224 to 239?
questions.e: Class D is reserved for multicast. Class E (240 to 255) is experimental.

questions.q: What is the default subnet mask of a Class B address such as 150.10.0.0?
questions.e: Classes A, B and C default to /8, /16 and /24.

questions.q: What does CIDR notation /24 mean?
o: The first 24 bits are the network portion
questions.e: The prefix length is the number of 1 bits in the mask.

questions.q: What is VLSM?
o: Using different subnet sizes within one network to avoid wasting addresses
questions.e: Variable Length Subnet Masking gives each subnet the size it needs, such as /30 for links and /24 for users.

questions.q: How many /26 subnets can you make from a /24?
questions.e: Borrowing 2 bits gives 2^2 = 4 subnets of 64 addresses each.

questions.q: Which is the first usable host in 172.16.8.0/22?
questions.e: /22 covers 172.16.8.0 to 172.16.11.255. The first usable is .8.1.

questions.q: Are hosts 192.168.5.65/27 and 192.168.5.94/27 on the same subnet?
o: No, they are in different /27 subnets
Only if the router allows it
questions.e: The /27 block 64 to 95 contains both addresses.

questions.q: Why must private addresses be translated before going on the internet?
o: Private ranges aren't routed on the internet, so NAT/PAT swaps them for a public address
questions.e: Many organisations reuse the same private ranges, so they can't be used publicly.

questions.q: How many usable hosts are in a /28?
questions.e: 2^4 = 16 addresses minus 2 = 14 usable.

questions.q: Which mask gives 126 usable hosts?
questions.e: /25 has 7 host bits: 128 addresses, 126 usable.

questions.q: A Linux machine can't get a DHCP lease. What address does it often show?
o: No IPv4 address (0.0.0.0), as many Linux setups don't use APIPA by default
questions.e: Windows and macOS self-assign APIPA. Many Linux setups simply have no IPv4 address, though some can be set to use link-local addressing.

questions.q: Which is the last usable host in 192.168.1.128/25?
questions.e: The subnet runs 128 to 255. 255 is the broadcast, so .254 is the last usable.

questions.q: What does a host do if a destination IP is not on its own subnet?
o: Sends the packet to its default gateway
questions.e: The subnet mask tells the host whether to deliver locally or via the gateway.

questions.q: How many addresses does 10.0.0.0/8 contain?
questions.e: /8 leaves 24 host bits: 2^24 = 16,777,216.

questions.q: What does software-defined networking (SDN) separate?
o: The control plane (decisions) from the data plane (forwarding)
questions.e: A central controller makes decisions, and switches and routers just forward traffic.

questions.q: What is SD-WAN mainly used for?
o: Managing WAN links (internet, MPLS, cellular) centrally and choosing the best path per application
questions.e: SD-WAN builds overlays across many link types and steers traffic by policy.

questions.q: What does VXLAN do?
o: Carries Layer 2 Ethernet frames inside UDP so Layer 2 networks can stretch across a Layer 3 network
questions.e: VXLAN extends virtual networks across data centres using a 24-bit ID, allowing about 16 million segments.

questions.q: What is the core idea of zero trust architecture?
o: Never trust, always verify: every user and device is checked for every request
questions.e: Zero trust uses strong authentication, least privilege and continuous monitoring regardless of location.

questions.q: What is SASE?
o: A cloud service combining networking (such as SD-WAN) with security services delivered at the edge
questions.e: Secure Access Service Edge joins WAN connectivity and security (SSE) in the cloud.

questions.q: Which services are typically part of SSE?
o: Secure web gateway, CASB, ZTNA and firewall as a service
questions.e: Security Service Edge is the security half of SASE.

questions.q: What is infrastructure as code (IaC)?
o: Defining and building infrastructure with code and templates, so it's repeatable and version-controlled
questions.e: IaC brings software practices like source control and testing to infrastructure.

questions.q: Why use source control (such as Git) for infrastructure code?
o: It tracks every change, allows rollback and supports review before changes go live
It stops all configuration drift on its own
questions.e: Version history and branching make infrastructure changes safer and auditable.

questions.q: How long is an IPv6 address?
questions.e: IPv6 uses 128 bits written as eight groups of four hex digits.

questions.q: Which is a valid shortened form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?
questions.e: Leading zeros can be dropped and one run of zero groups replaced by :: once only.

questions.q: What does dual stack mean?
o: Devices run IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time
questions.e: Dual stack is the most common transition method while both protocols are in use.

questions.q: Which transition method lets IPv6-only clients reach IPv4-only servers by translating between them?
questions.e: NAT64 (usually with DNS64) translates IPv6 packets to IPv4 and back.

questions.q: What do IPv6 tunnelling methods such as 6to4 do?
o: Carry IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets across an IPv4 network
questions.e: Tunnelling lets IPv6 islands talk across IPv4-only networks.

questions.q: Why was IPv6 created?
o: IPv4 public addresses were running out
questions.e: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses. IPv6's 128-bit space is vastly larger.

questions.q: In SDN, what does the southbound API do?
o: Lets the controller program the switches and routers
questions.e: Northbound APIs face applications and automation tools. Southbound APIs face the network devices.

questions.q: A company wants new branch networks built identically every time from templates. What approach fits?
o: Infrastructure as code with automation playbooks
questions.e: Automation and templates prevent configuration drift and human error.

questions.q: Which IPv6 address is the loopback?
questions.e: ::1 is loopback. fe80:: is link-local and ff02:: addresses are multicast.

questions.q: Which IPv6 address type starts with fe80 and only works on the local link?
questions.e: Every IPv6 interface has a link-local address for local communication.

questions.q: Under zero trust, a user who has logged in from the office:
o: Is still verified for each resource, with least privilege applied
questions.e: Location on the network doesn't grant trust in a zero trust model.

questions.q: An organisation's IPv6-only mobile network must let users reach websites that only have IPv4 addresses. What is commonly used?
questions.e: DNS64 creates synthetic IPv6 addresses for IPv4-only sites, and NAT64 translates the traffic.

questions.q: What is a static route?
o: A route an administrator enters manually
A route that changes every minute
questions.e: Static routes are simple and predictable but don't adapt to failures unless you configure backups.

questions.q: Which routing protocol is used between organisations on the internet?
questions.e: BGP is the exterior gateway protocol of the internet, routing between autonomous systems.

questions.q: Which routing protocol is a link-state protocol that uses cost based on bandwidth?
questions.e: OSPF builds a map of the network and picks the lowest total cost path.

questions.q: Which routing protocol is Cisco-developed and uses bandwidth and delay in its metric?
questions.e: EIGRP is an advanced distance-vector protocol, now partly open but mainly used on Cisco gear.

questions.q: A router has routes to 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.1.5.0/24. Which does it use for a packet to 10.1.5.20?
o: 10.1.5.0/24, because the longest prefix match wins
questions.e: The most specific route (longest prefix) is chosen first, before administrative distance or metric come into it.

questions.q: What does administrative distance (AD) measure?
o: How trustworthy a route source is; lower is preferred
The physical distance to the router
questions.e: When two sources offer the same prefix, the router prefers the lower AD (for example static 1, OSPF 110).

questions.q: Which has the lower (more trusted) administrative distance on Cisco routers by default?
questions.e: Directly connected is 0 and static is 1, so they beat routing protocols.

questions.q: What is a floating static route?
o: A backup static route with a higher administrative distance, used only if the main route fails
A route that moves between routers
A route with no next hop
questions.e: Setting a higher AD (for example 200) keeps it out of the table until the primary disappears.

questions.q: When two routes have the same prefix length and administrative distance, what decides between them?
questions.e: The metric (cost, hop count, bandwidth and delay) picks the best path within one protocol.

questions.q: What does PAT do?
o: Lets many internal hosts share one public IP by tracking different source ports
Gives every host its own public IP
questions.e: Port Address Translation (NAT overload) is what home routers use.

questions.q: What is the main difference between static NAT and PAT?
o: Static NAT maps one private IP to one public IP; PAT maps many private IPs to one public IP using ports
questions.e: Static NAT is used for servers that need a fixed public address.

questions.q: What does a first hop redundancy protocol (FHRP) provide?
o: A virtual default gateway shared by two or more routers, so hosts keep working if one fails
questions.e: HSRP, VRRP and GLBP give hosts one virtual IP and MAC as their gateway.

questions.q: In an FHRP setup, what do hosts use as their default gateway?
o: The virtual IP (VIP) shared by the routers
Each router's real IP in turn
questions.e: If the active router fails, the standby takes over the VIP and hosts don't notice.

questions.q: What is a router subinterface used for?
o: Dividing one physical interface into logical interfaces, such as for router-on-a-stick inter-VLAN routing
questions.e: Each subinterface carries one VLAN's traffic using 802.1Q tags.

questions.q: Which routing protocol treats each autonomous system as a hop and chooses paths based on attributes and policy?
questions.e: BGP is a path-vector protocol, focused on policy rather than speed.

questions.q: A small office has one internet connection. What single route is usually enough to send all non-local traffic to the ISP?
questions.e: The default route matches anything without a more specific route.

questions.q: Which protocol uses hop count as its only metric and has a maximum of 15 hops?
questions.e: RIP is simple but slow to converge and limited in size, so it's rarely used now.

questions.q: What is convergence in routing?
o: All routers agreeing on the network's routes after a change
questions.e: Faster convergence means less disruption after a link fails.

questions.q: Which FHRP is an open standard?
questions.e: VRRP is open. HSRP and GLBP are Cisco protocols.

questions.q: Users behind a router all appear to websites as the same public IP. What feature is in use?
questions.e: PAT translates many inside addresses to one outside address.

questions.q: Which command shows a router's routing table on Cisco devices?
questions.e: The routing table lists known networks, how they were learned and the next hop.

questions.q: What does a VLAN do?
o: Splits one physical switch into separate logical networks (broadcast domains)
questions.e: Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain. Traffic between VLANs needs routing.

questions.q: Which standard adds VLAN tags to Ethernet frames on trunk links?
questions.e: 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag carrying the VLAN ID.

questions.q: What is the native VLAN on an 802.1Q trunk?
o: The VLAN whose traffic crosses the trunk untagged
A VLAN that is always disabled
questions.e: Untagged frames on a trunk belong to the native VLAN. Mismatched native VLANs cause problems.

questions.q: Why should the native VLAN be changed from VLAN 1 to an unused VLAN?
o: To make VLAN hopping (double tagging) attacks harder
questions.e: Using an unused native VLAN and tagging it reduces the risk of double-tagging attacks.

questions.q: An IP phone and a PC share one switch port. How are their traffic types kept separate?
o: The port has a data VLAN for the PC and a voice VLAN for the phone
The PC is set to half duplex
questions.e: A voice VLAN lets QoS treat call traffic separately from data.

questions.q: What is a switched virtual interface (SVI)?
o: A virtual Layer 3 interface for a VLAN on a switch, often used as that VLAN's gateway
questions.e: SVIs let multilayer switches route between VLANs.

questions.q: What does link aggregation (LACP / 802.3ad) do?
o: Combines several physical links into one logical link for more bandwidth and redundancy
questions.e: Port channels act as one link, so spanning tree doesn't block the extra cables.

questions.q: What problem does spanning tree protocol (STP) prevent?
questions.e: STP blocks redundant paths and unblocks them if the active path fails.

questions.q: How is the STP root bridge chosen?
o: The switch with the lowest bridge ID (priority, then MAC address)
The switch with the most ports
questions.e: Set the priority on the switch you want as root, rather than leaving it to the lowest MAC.

questions.q: Which port state does STP put a redundant link into to stop loops?
questions.e: Blocked ports discard frames but still listen for BPDUs, so they can take over if needed.

questions.q: What is the standard Ethernet MTU?
questions.e: Frames carrying more than 1500 bytes of payload are jumbo frames.

questions.q: Why might a storage network use jumbo frames (around 9000 bytes)?
o: Fewer, larger frames reduce overhead for big data transfers
questions.e: Every device on the path must support the same jumbo MTU, or frames are dropped or fragmented.

questions.q: A switch port is set to 100 Mbps full duplex and the PC is set to auto. The link is slow with many errors. What is likely?
questions.e: Hard-coding one side and auto on the other can give a duplex mismatch. Set both to auto or both to the same values.

questions.q: What is the difference between an access port and a trunk port?
o: An access port carries one VLAN untagged; a trunk carries multiple VLANs with tags
An access port carries more VLANs
questions.e: Trunks link switches to switches, routers or hypervisors.

questions.q: Two switches are joined by a trunk, but PCs in VLAN 30 on different switches can't communicate. Others can. What should you check?
o: Whether VLAN 30 is allowed on the trunk and exists on both switches
questions.e: Trunks can prune VLANs, and a VLAN must exist in each switch's VLAN database.

questions.q: What does a switch do with a frame for a MAC address it hasn't learned yet?
o: Floods it out every port in that VLAN except the one it came in on
questions.e: Once the destination replies, the switch learns its port and forwards directly.

questions.q: What does the VLAN database on a switch hold?
o: The list of VLANs configured on that switch
questions.e: Ports can only be assigned to VLANs that exist in the database.

questions.q: Why does inter-VLAN traffic need a router or Layer 3 switch?
o: Each VLAN is a separate network, and traffic between networks must be routed
questions.e: Router-on-a-stick or SVIs on a multilayer switch handle routing between VLANs.

questions.q: Which statement about link aggregation is correct?
o: Both ends must be configured to match, such as with LACP
questions.e: LACP negotiates the bundle. Mismatched settings can cause the links to be blocked or error-disabled.

questions.q: Rapid spanning tree (802.1w) improves on classic STP by:
o: Converging much faster after a topology change
questions.e: RSTP converges in seconds rather than up to 50 seconds.

questions.q: A network admin wants a port to stop forwarding if it detects a loop from a user plugging in a cheap switch. Which feature helps?
questions.e: BPDU guard error-disables an access port that receives BPDUs.

questions.q: Which 2.4 GHz channels don't overlap, in most regions?
questions.e: Using only 1, 6 and 11 avoids co-channel interference between neighbouring APs. (Channel 14 is Japan-only and 802.11b only.)

questions.q: What does band steering do?
o: Encourages dual-band clients onto the faster, less crowded 5 GHz or 6 GHz band
questions.e: APs can delay or redirect probe responses on 2.4 GHz to nudge capable clients to higher bands.

questions.q: What is the difference between an SSID and a BSSID?
o: The SSID is the network name; the BSSID is the MAC address of the AP radio serving it
The SSID is a VLAN ID
questions.e: Several APs can share an SSID (an ESS), each with its own BSSID.

questions.q: Several access points share one network name so users can roam. What is this called?
questions.e: An ESS joins multiple BSSs under one SSID for seamless roaming.

questions.q: Which wireless mode connects devices directly to each other with no access point?
questions.e: Ad hoc networks are peer-to-peer and rarely used in businesses.

questions.q: Two buildings 300 metres apart need a wireless link. Which antenna type suits this best?
o: Directional antennas pointed at each other
questions.e: Directional antennas focus the signal in one direction for long point-to-point links.

questions.q: Which wireless security option uses SAE and is the most secure for home networks?
questions.e: WPA3 replaces the pre-shared key handshake with SAE, which resists offline guessing.

questions.q: What is the main difference between PSK and enterprise Wi-Fi authentication?
o: PSK uses one shared password; enterprise uses individual logins checked by a RADIUS server (802.1X)
questions.e: Enterprise lets you revoke one user without changing everyone's password.

questions.q: A café wants guests to accept terms before using Wi-Fi. What should it use?
o: A captive portal on a guest network
questions.e: Captive portals show a web page that guests must complete before getting access.

questions.q: What is a lightweight access point?
o: One managed centrally by a wireless LAN controller rather than configured on its own
An AP that only does 2.4 GHz
questions.e: Autonomous APs are configured individually. Lightweight APs get their settings from a controller.

questions.q: What does 802.11h add to 5 GHz Wi-Fi?
o: Dynamic frequency selection and transmit power control to avoid interfering with radar
questions.e: 802.11h helps APs comply with regulations by moving off channels where radar is detected.

questions.q: Which frequency band was added by Wi-Fi 6E?
questions.e: 6 GHz offers many wide, non-overlapping channels but shorter range.

questions.q: What is a downside of using a wide 160 MHz channel?
o: Fewer non-overlapping channels and more chance of interference
questions.e: Wider channels carry more data but use up more of the band.

questions.q: Why should a guest Wi-Fi network be isolated from the corporate network?
o: So untrusted devices can't reach internal systems
questions.e: Guest networks usually sit in their own VLAN with internet-only access.

questions.q: Which antenna type spreads signal in all directions horizontally, suiting an AP in the middle of an office?
questions.e: Omni antennas cover all around the AP, good for general coverage.

questions.q: In a mesh Wi-Fi network:
o: Access points connect to each other wirelessly to extend coverage without cabling every AP
questions.e: Mesh suits large or hard-to-cable areas, though wireless backhaul reduces throughput.

questions.q: Which 802.11 standard is Wi-Fi 6?
questions.e: 802.11n is Wi-Fi 4, ac is Wi-Fi 5, ax is Wi-Fi 6/6E and be is Wi-Fi 7.

questions.q: Which is a weakness of WPA2-Personal compared with WPA3-Personal?
o: Captured handshakes can be attacked offline to guess the passphrase
It has no encryption at all
questions.e: WPA3's SAE stops offline dictionary attacks against captured handshakes.

questions.q: An office AP is set to channel 6, and a neighbour's AP is also on channel 6. What is the likely effect?
o: Co-channel interference, so both networks share airtime and slow down
questions.e: APs on the same channel take turns to transmit. Choose a clear channel with a Wi-Fi analyser.

questions.q: Which wireless topology links exactly two sites, such as two buildings?
questions.e: Point-to-point bridges usually use directional antennas.

questions.q: Which is true of the 5 GHz band compared with 2.4 GHz?
o: More non-overlapping channels and less interference, but shorter range
questions.e: Higher frequencies give more capacity but don't pass through walls as well.

questions.q: Which channel width is usually recommended on 2.4 GHz?
questions.e: Wider channels on 2.4 GHz overlap neighbours and cause interference.

questions.q: What is the difference between an MDF and an IDF?
o: The MDF is the main distribution room where external lines enter; IDFs serve individual floors or areas
An IDF connects to the ISP directly
The MDF is only for power
questions.e: Horizontal cabling runs from user areas to an IDF, and IDFs connect back to the MDF.

questions.q: Why should rack equipment's airflow direction match the rack's hot and cold aisles?
o: So cool air is drawn in from the cold aisle and hot air exhausted into the hot aisle
questions.e: Mixing port-side intake and exhaust devices recirculates hot air and causes overheating.

questions.q: How tall is a standard rack unit (1U)?
questions.e: A 42U rack holds 42 units of 1.75 inches each.

questions.q: What is a PDU in a rack?
o: A power distribution unit that supplies power outlets to rack equipment
questions.e: Rack PDUs can be basic or managed, with remote monitoring and switching of outlets.

questions.q: What does a UPS provide?
o: Battery power during an outage, long enough for a safe shutdown or a generator to start
questions.e: UPSs also condition power, protecting against sags and surges.

questions.q: What is a fibre distribution panel used for?
o: Terminating and organising fibre runs so they can be patched to equipment
questions.e: Like a copper patch panel, it protects fibre ends and makes moves and changes easier.

questions.q: Which fire suppression method is preferred in server rooms?
o: A clean agent gas system that doesn't damage electronics
questions.e: Clean agents put out fires without leaving residue. Water would destroy equipment.

questions.q: Why is humidity monitored in a data centre?
o: Too low increases static discharge; too high causes condensation and corrosion
questions.e: Keeping humidity in range protects equipment from both risks.

questions.q: A rack has a 20 A circuit. Why shouldn't you load it to the full 20 A continuously?
o: Circuits shouldn't run at more than about 80% of their rating continuously, to avoid overheating and trips
It will speed up the servers
questions.e: Plan power load with headroom, using watts = volts x amps to calculate draw.

questions.q: Why fit lockable racks and cabinets?
o: To stop unauthorised people tampering with network equipment
questions.e: Physical security of network gear matters as much as logical security.

questions.q: What is a patch panel for?
o: Terminating structured cabling runs so short patch leads can connect them to switches
questions.e: Patch panels make it easy to move connections without re-running cables.

questions.q: Which statement about rack depth and size is correct?
o: Racks come in different heights (in U) and depths, chosen to fit the equipment and room
All racks are the same size
Rack size only matters for Wi-Fi
questions.e: Server racks are often deeper than network-only racks.

questions.q: Many UPSs list two ratings, VA and watts. Which should you check against your equipment's power draw?
o: Watts, as that's the real power the UPS can supply
questions.e: VA is apparent power. Make sure the total wattage of your equipment fits the UPS's watt rating.

questions.q: Where is the demarcation point (demarc) usually found?
o: Where the ISP's responsibility ends and the customer's begins, often in the MDF
questions.e: Problems on the provider side of the demarc are the ISP's to fix.

questions.q: What is structured cabling?
o: A standardised way of organising a building's cabling into defined elements and spaces
questions.e: Standards make networks easier to document, expand and troubleshoot.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a physical and a logical network diagram?
o: A physical diagram shows where devices and cables actually are; a logical one shows how data flows, such as subnets and VLANs
A logical diagram shows rack positions
A physical diagram shows IP addresses only
questions.e: Technicians use physical diagrams to find equipment and logical diagrams to trace traffic.

questions.q: Which document shows exactly which device sits in each position of an equipment rack?
questions.e: Rack diagrams show each device's location by U position.

questions.q: What does a wireless heat map show?
o: Wi-Fi signal strength across a floor plan
questions.e: Heat maps from site surveys reveal dead spots and overlapping coverage.

questions.q: What is IPAM?
o: IP address management: tracking how address space is allocated and used
questions.e: IPAM tools track subnets, DHCP scopes, reservations and DNS records to prevent conflicts.

questions.q: What does a service-level agreement (SLA) define?
o: The level of service a provider commits to, such as uptime and response times
questions.e: SLAs set measurable targets and what happens if they're missed.

questions.q: A switch model has reached end of support (EOS). What does that mean?
o: The vendor no longer provides updates, patches or support for it
questions.e: EOS devices become a security risk, so plan replacements before that date.

questions.q: What is the difference between end of life (EOL) and end of support (EOS)?
o: EOL usually means it's no longer sold; EOS means updates and support have stopped
They mean exactly the same thing
EOL means the device is broken
questions.e: Vendors typically announce EOL first, then stop support some time later.

questions.q: What is a golden configuration?
o: A trusted, approved baseline configuration used as the standard for devices
questions.e: Golden configs make deployments consistent and help spot unauthorised changes.

questions.q: Why keep backup copies of device configurations?
o: To restore a device quickly after a failure or a bad change
questions.e: Config backups should be taken regularly and stored securely off the device.

questions.q: What is the purpose of change management?
o: To plan, approve, test and document changes so they don't cause unexpected outages
questions.e: Changes go through a request, risk assessment, approval, scheduled window and rollback plan.

questions.q: Before a firmware upgrade on core switches, what should be in the change request?
o: The plan, risk, maintenance window and a rollback plan
questions.e: A rollback plan is essential in case the upgrade fails.

questions.q: What is an asset inventory?
o: A full list of an organisation's hardware and software with details such as location and owner
questions.e: Inventories support lifecycle planning, audits and security.

questions.q: Which diagram focuses on Layer 3, showing subnets, routers and how networks connect?
questions.e: Layer 1 diagrams show cabling, Layer 2 shows switching and VLANs, and Layer 3 shows routing and IP addressing.

questions.q: What is the production configuration of a device?
o: The configuration currently running in live use
questions.e: Compare production configs against the golden baseline to catch drift.

questions.q: A cable map (port map) helps technicians:
o: Match wall jacks to patch panel ports and switch ports
questions.e: Labelled jacks and an up-to-date port map speed up moves and troubleshooting.

questions.q: Why should patching and firmware updates be part of lifecycle management?
o: They fix vulnerabilities and bugs over the device's working life
They aren't needed on network gear
questions.e: Firmware on switches, routers and APs needs regular updates like any OS.

questions.q: What should happen to network devices during decommissioning?
o: Wipe configurations and data securely, update inventory, then dispose or recycle properly
Give them to staff without checks
questions.e: Configs can contain passwords and network details useful to attackers.

questions.q: What does an SNMP trap do?
o: Lets an agent send an alert to the manager straight away when something happens
Lets the manager poll an agent
questions.e: Traps (UDP 162) are unsolicited alerts. Polling uses UDP 161.

questions.q: What is an SNMP MIB?
o: A database describing the information (OIDs) a device can report
questions.e: The Management Information Base defines what can be monitored on a device.

questions.q: Why is SNMPv3 preferred over v2c?
o: It adds proper authentication and encryption, using usernames rather than community strings
questions.e: v1 and v2c send community strings in clear text. v3 provides authentication and privacy.

questions.q: What is an SNMP community string?
o: A shared, plain-text value acting as a password between v1/v2c managers and agents
questions.e: Change default community strings like 'public' and 'private', or better, use v3.

questions.q: What does flow data (such as NetFlow) show?
o: Summaries of who talked to whom, using which ports and how much data
questions.e: Flow records are lighter than full captures and great for spotting top talkers and unusual traffic.

questions.q: When would you use a full packet capture rather than flow data?
o: When you need to see the actual contents of the traffic to diagnose a problem
To see bandwidth trends over a year
questions.e: Captures show every byte but take a lot of storage.

questions.q: What is a network baseline?
o: A record of normal performance used to spot unusual behaviour
questions.e: Alerts can fire when metrics move away from the baseline.

questions.q: What does a SIEM do?
o: Collects logs from many sources, correlates events and raises security alerts
questions.e: Security information and event management centralises and analyses logs.

questions.q: Why send device logs to a central syslog server?
o: To keep them in one place for searching and correlation, even if a device is compromised or reset
questions.e: Log aggregation makes troubleshooting and investigations much easier.

questions.q: What is port mirroring (SPAN) used for?
o: Copying traffic from one port to another so a monitoring tool can analyse it
questions.e: An IDS or protocol analyser connected to the mirror port sees a copy of the traffic.

questions.q: What is the benefit of monitoring tools integrating via APIs?
o: They can pull data from and push actions to other systems automatically
They remove the need for logins
questions.e: APIs let monitoring link with ticketing, cloud platforms and automation.

questions.q: What is scheduled network discovery?
o: Automatically scanning the network at set times to find new or changed devices
A manual audit once a decade
questions.e: Discovery keeps inventory and monitoring up to date. Ad hoc discovery runs on demand.

questions.q: Which type of monitoring checks whether a service is up and reachable?
questions.e: Availability checks track uptime and downtime of devices and services.

questions.q: What does configuration monitoring do?
o: Watches for changes to device configurations and alerts on unexpected ones
questions.e: Unexpected changes can mean mistakes or an attacker.

questions.q: An admin wants alerts when a switch's interface errors climb above normal. What do they need first?
o: A performance baseline for that interface
questions.e: You can't spot abnormal without knowing what normal looks like.

questions.q: Which tool would show which hosts are using the most bandwidth over the past week?
questions.e: Flow tools report top talkers, applications and conversations over time.

questions.q: What does RPO (recovery point objective) measure?
o: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time
questions.e: An RPO of 1 hour means backups must be frequent enough that no more than an hour's data is lost.

questions.q: What does RTO (recovery time objective) measure?
o: The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after a disaster
How much data can be lost
questions.e: RTO is about downtime. RPO is about data loss.

questions.q: What does MTTR stand for and measure?
o: Mean time to repair: the average time to fix a failed component
questions.e: Lower MTTR means quicker recovery from failures.

questions.q: What does MTBF measure?
o: Mean time between failures for repairable equipment
questions.e: A higher MTBF means more reliable equipment.

questions.q: Which recovery site is fully equipped and ready to take over almost immediately?
questions.e: Hot sites are the most expensive but give the shortest recovery time.

questions.q: Which recovery site has space and power but little or no equipment set up?
questions.e: Cold sites are cheapest but take the longest to bring online.

questions.q: Which recovery site has some equipment and connectivity, needing data and final setup before use?
questions.e: Warm sites balance cost and recovery time.

questions.q: What is an active-active high availability setup?
o: Both systems handle traffic at the same time and share the load
One system waits idle until the other fails
questions.e: In active-passive, the standby only takes over on failure.

questions.q: What is a tabletop exercise?
o: A discussion-based walk-through of the DR plan with the team, without touching systems
questions.e: Tabletops find gaps in plans and responsibilities cheaply.

questions.q: What is validation testing in DR?
o: Actually testing that recovery steps and systems work, such as restoring backups or failing over
questions.e: Validation proves the plan works in practice, not just on paper.

questions.q: A business can lose at most 15 minutes of transactions. Which metric does this set?
questions.e: Data loss tolerance is the recovery point objective.

questions.q: An online shop must be back up within 2 hours of an outage. Which metric is this?
questions.e: Time to restore service is the recovery time objective.

questions.q: Which HA design is usually cheaper but has a short delay while the standby takes over?
questions.e: The passive node sits idle until failover, so there may be a brief interruption.

questions.q: Why is MTTF used instead of MTBF for some items?
o: MTTF is for items that are replaced rather than repaired
questions.e: Mean time to failure suits non-repairable parts such as drives or fans.

questions.q: Which site type gives the fastest recovery but at the highest cost?
questions.e: Hot sites have live systems and up-to-date data ready to go.

questions.q: What is a DHCP reservation?
o: A fixed IP that DHCP always gives to a specific device, matched by MAC address
An address range excluded from DHCP
questions.e: Reservations suit printers and servers that need a stable address but are still managed by DHCP.

questions.q: What is a DHCP exclusion?
o: Addresses inside a scope that DHCP won't hand out, for statically assigned devices
questions.e: Exclusions stop DHCP clashing with static addresses on routers, servers and printers.

questions.q: Clients on VLAN 20 can't get DHCP addresses, but the DHCP server is on VLAN 10. What is needed?
o: A DHCP relay (IP helper) on the VLAN 20 gateway
questions.e: DHCP discovery is a broadcast, which routers don't forward. A relay forwards it as unicast to the server.

questions.q: When does a DHCP client first try to renew its lease?
questions.e: If the original server doesn't answer, the client tries any server at 87.5%.

questions.q: What is a DHCP scope?
o: The range of addresses and options a DHCP server can hand out for a subnet
questions.e: Scopes include the range, mask, lease time and options such as gateway and DNS servers.

questions.q: Which DHCP options are commonly given to clients?
o: Default gateway, DNS servers and domain name
questions.e: Options save configuring each client by hand.

questions.q: What is SLAAC?
o: IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration, where hosts build their own address from router advertisements
questions.e: Hosts take the network prefix from the router and create the host part themselves.

questions.q: Which DNS record maps a name to an IPv6 address?
questions.e: A records hold IPv4 addresses. AAAA (quad A) records hold IPv6.

questions.q: Which DNS record is used for reverse lookups, mapping an IP to a name?
questions.e: PTR records live in reverse lookup zones.

questions.q: Which DNS record tells other servers where to deliver a domain's email?
questions.e: MX records point to mail servers, with priorities.

questions.q: Which DNS record type holds free text, often used for SPF, DKIM and domain verification?
questions.e: TXT records carry text used by email security and other services.

questions.q: Which DNS record identifies the name servers that are authoritative for a zone?
questions.e: NS records delegate a zone to its DNS servers.

questions.q: What is a CNAME record?
o: An alias that points one name to another name
questions.e: For example, www.example.com can be a CNAME for example.com.

questions.q: What does DNSSEC add to DNS?
o: Digital signatures so resolvers can check answers haven't been tampered with
questions.e: DNSSEC protects integrity (against spoofing). DoH and DoT protect privacy by encrypting queries.

questions.q: What is the difference between DoH and DoT?
o: DoH sends DNS over HTTPS (port 443); DoT sends DNS over TLS on port 853
questions.e: Both encrypt DNS queries so others on the network can't read or alter them.

questions.q: What is an authoritative DNS answer?
o: One that comes from a server holding the actual zone for that domain
A cached answer from another server
An answer from the hosts file
questions.e: Non-authoritative answers come from a resolver's cache.

questions.q: What does a recursive DNS server do?
o: Does the full lookup for the client, querying other servers until it finds the answer
Only answers for its own zone
questions.e: Clients usually send recursive queries to their configured resolver.

questions.q: What is the difference between a primary and a secondary DNS server for a zone?
o: The primary holds the editable zone; secondaries hold read-only copies kept up to date by zone transfers
The primary is only for reverse lookups
questions.e: Secondaries add redundancy and spread the load.

questions.q: Which file on a PC is checked for name resolution before DNS and can override it?
questions.e: Malware sometimes edits the hosts file to redirect sites.

questions.q: Which protocol gives much more precise time than NTP, used in finance and telecoms?
questions.e: PTP can reach sub-microsecond accuracy, often with hardware timestamping.

questions.q: What does NTS add to NTP?
o: Network Time Security: authentication so clients can trust time sources
questions.e: NTS protects against attackers feeding false time.

questions.q: What does NTP stratum 1 mean?
o: A server directly connected to an accurate reference clock (stratum 0), such as GPS or an atomic clock
questions.e: Each step further from the reference adds one to the stratum number.

questions.q: What is a site-to-site VPN?
o: A permanent tunnel joining two networks, such as an office and a data centre, through their routers or firewalls
questions.e: Users at each site don't need any VPN software.

questions.q: What is a split-tunnel VPN?
o: Only traffic for the company network goes through the VPN; other traffic goes straight to the internet
All traffic goes through the VPN
questions.e: Split tunnel saves bandwidth. Full tunnel sends everything through the company for inspection.

questions.q: Why might a company require a full-tunnel VPN?
o: So all of a remote user's traffic passes through company security controls
questions.e: Full tunnel gives more visibility and protection at the cost of bandwidth.

questions.q: What is a clientless VPN?
o: A VPN accessed through a web browser, with no VPN software installed
questions.e: Clientless (SSL/TLS) VPNs give access to web-based resources through a portal.

questions.q: What is a jump box (jump host)?
o: A hardened server admins connect to first, and then from it to sensitive systems
questions.e: Jump boxes limit and log admin access to protected networks.

questions.q: What is out-of-band management?
o: Managing devices over a separate network or connection, such as a console server or modem, so access works even if the main network is down
Managing devices over the production network
questions.e: In-band management uses the same network as user traffic.

questions.q: Which method gives direct access to a new switch with no IP address configured?
questions.e: Console access works locally with no network configuration.

questions.q: Why use SSH instead of Telnet to manage network devices?
o: SSH encrypts the session, including passwords
questions.e: Telnet sends everything in clear text.

questions.q: What is an advantage of managing devices through an API?
o: Changes can be automated and scripted across many devices
questions.e: APIs support automation and tools like infrastructure as code.

questions.q: A core switch has crashed and the management network is down. How can an engineer still reach it?
o: Through out-of-band management, such as a console server
questions.e: OOB access is designed for exactly this situation.

questions.q: Which is a client-to-site VPN?
o: A remote worker's laptop connecting to the office network
questions.e: Client-to-site (remote access) VPNs connect individual devices.

questions.q: Why place a jump box in its own secured segment?
o: So admin access to sensitive systems is controlled, monitored and logged in one place
questions.e: Only the jump box is allowed to reach the protected systems' management interfaces.

questions.q: Which is in-band management?
o: Using SSH over the normal production network
Using a console server on a separate line
questions.e: In-band shares the network that users rely on.

questions.q: What is a GUI used for in network management?
o: Managing a device through a graphical web or desktop interface
questions.e: Many devices offer a web GUI alongside the command line.

questions.q: Which VPN type suits giving a contractor browser-only access to one internal web app?
questions.e: Clientless portals avoid installing software on the contractor's device.

questions.q: What does the CIA triad stand for?
questions.e: Security controls aim to keep data private, accurate and available when needed.

questions.q: Which part of the CIA triad does a DDoS attack mainly target?
questions.e: DDoS stops legitimate users reaching a service.

questions.q: What is the difference between encrypting data in transit and at rest?
o: In transit protects data moving across a network; at rest protects stored data
At rest only applies to Wi-Fi
In transit only applies to backups
questions.e: TLS and VPNs protect data in transit. Disk encryption protects data at rest.

questions.q: What is a self-signed certificate?
o: A certificate signed by its own creator rather than a trusted certificate authority
A certificate from a public CA
questions.e: Browsers don't trust self-signed certificates by default. They're fine for internal testing.

questions.q: What is PKI?
o: The system of certificate authorities, certificates and keys used to establish trust
questions.e: Public key infrastructure issues, validates and revokes certificates.

questions.q: Which protocol provides centralised authentication for network access, such as enterprise Wi-Fi and VPNs?
questions.e: RADIUS works with 802.1X so each user logs in with their own credentials.

questions.q: What is a key advantage of TACACS+ over RADIUS for device administration?
o: It separates authentication, authorisation and accounting and encrypts the whole session
questions.e: TACACS+ (TCP 49) is common for controlling admin access to network devices.

questions.q: What does SAML enable?
o: Single sign-on to web applications by passing authentication assertions from an identity provider
questions.e: Users log in once with the identity provider and access many web apps.

questions.q: What is role-based access control (RBAC)?
o: Granting permissions based on a person's job role
Access based on time of day only
questions.e: RBAC makes permissions easier to manage and supports least privilege.

questions.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
o: Giving users only the access they need to do their job
questions.e: It limits the damage from mistakes and compromised accounts.

questions.q: What is geofencing in network security?
o: Allowing or blocking access based on a device's location
A physical fence round a data centre
questions.e: For example, block logins from countries the company doesn't operate in.

questions.q: What is a honeypot?
o: A decoy system designed to attract attackers so their behaviour can be studied
questions.e: A honeynet is a network of honeypots.

questions.q: What is the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit?
o: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is a method that takes advantage of it
questions.e: A threat is anything that could take advantage of a vulnerability. Risk combines likelihood and impact.

questions.q: Which regulation protects the personal data of people in the UK and EU?
questions.e: GDPR covers how personal data is collected, stored and processed.

questions.q: Which standard must organisations follow if they handle card payments?
questions.e: PCI DSS sets security requirements for cardholder data.

questions.q: What does data locality refer to?
o: Rules on which country or region data must be stored and processed in
How close data is to the CPU
questions.e: Some laws require data to stay within certain borders.

questions.q: Why should IoT devices be put on their own network segment?
o: They're often poorly secured, so isolating them limits what an attacker can reach
questions.e: Segmentation also applies to SCADA/ICS/OT, guest and BYOD devices.

questions.q: Why should SCADA and industrial control systems be strongly segmented from the office network?
o: Compromise could affect physical processes and safety, and many can't be patched easily
questions.e: OT networks are often isolated or tightly controlled with firewalls.

questions.q: Which is an example of MFA?
o: A password plus a code from an authenticator app
questions.e: MFA needs factors from different categories: something you know, have or are.

questions.q: What is time-based authentication?
o: Allowing logins only at certain times, or using codes that change over time
questions.e: Examples are restricting access to working hours or using TOTP codes.

questions.q: What physical security controls protect network equipment?
o: Locks, badge access and security cameras
questions.e: Physical access can bypass many logical controls, so rooms and racks must be secured.

questions.q: What is a DDoS attack?
o: Many compromised systems flood a target so legitimate users can't reach it
questions.e: Distributed attacks often use botnets, making them hard to block by source.

questions.q: How does a VLAN hopping attack using double tagging work?
o: The attacker adds two VLAN tags; the first switch strips the native VLAN tag and the frame is forwarded into another VLAN
It floods the switch with MAC addresses
It sets up a fake access point
questions.e: Using an unused native VLAN and tagging it stops double tagging.

questions.q: What does a MAC flooding attack try to do?
o: Fill the switch's MAC table so it floods frames out every port, letting the attacker see traffic
questions.e: Port security limiting MAC addresses per port prevents this.

questions.q: What is ARP poisoning?
o: Sending false ARP replies so traffic for another IP (such as the gateway) goes to the attacker
questions.e: It's a common way to set up an on-path (man-in-the-middle) attack. Dynamic ARP inspection helps prevent it.

questions.q: What is DNS poisoning?
o: Corrupting DNS data so users are sent to the wrong (malicious) IP address
questions.e: DNSSEC helps protect against forged DNS answers.

questions.q: What is a rogue DHCP server?
o: An unauthorised DHCP server handing out wrong settings, such as a malicious gateway or DNS server
questions.e: DHCP snooping lets only trusted ports send DHCP offers.

questions.q: What is an evil twin?
o: A fake access point using the same SSID as a real one to trick users into connecting
questions.e: Users connected to an evil twin can have their traffic watched or credentials stolen.

questions.q: An employee plugs a cheap wireless router into a wall socket to get better Wi-Fi. What is this?
questions.e: Rogue APs bypass security controls. Wireless intrusion prevention and NAC can detect them.

questions.q: What is an on-path attack?
o: The attacker secretly intercepts, and possibly changes, traffic between two parties
questions.e: It was formerly called man-in-the-middle.

questions.q: Someone follows an employee through a secure door without badging in. What is this?
questions.e: Access control vestibules and staff awareness help prevent it.

questions.q: An attacker watches a user type their password at a reception desk. What is this?
questions.e: Privacy screens and awareness help.

questions.q: An attacker searches a company's bins for printed network diagrams. What is this?
questions.e: Shred sensitive documents before disposal.

questions.q: Staff receive an email that looks like it's from IT, asking them to log in at a link to 'keep their account'. What is this?
questions.e: Phishing tricks users into giving away credentials or running malware.

questions.q: Which malware type encrypts files and demands payment?
questions.e: Offline, tested backups are the key defence.

questions.q: Which malware spreads across a network by itself, without user action?
questions.e: Worms exploit vulnerabilities to copy themselves from host to host.

questions.q: Which defence stops a user's PC accepting fake gateway MAC addresses from ARP spoofing?
o: Dynamic ARP inspection on the switch
questions.e: DAI checks ARP packets against DHCP snooping records.

questions.q: What is DNS spoofing?
o: Sending forged DNS responses so a victim gets the wrong IP for a name
questions.e: Spoofing fakes answers. Poisoning corrupts stored records or caches.

questions.q: Users report they keep getting IP addresses in a range nobody recognises, with a strange gateway. What is likely?
o: A rogue DHCP server on the network
questions.e: Find and remove it, and enable DHCP snooping.

questions.q: Which attack against a switch is stopped by limiting how many MAC addresses a port can learn?
questions.e: Port security can shut down or restrict a port that exceeds its MAC limit.

questions.q: What is a malicious charging cable attack?
o: A cable that looks normal but contains hardware to inject keystrokes or steal data when plugged in
questions.e: Only use trusted cables and chargers, and be wary of found or gifted ones.

questions.q: Which is a basic device hardening step?
o: Disable unused ports and services and change default passwords
questions.e: Hardening reduces the attack surface of each device.

questions.q: What does 802.1X provide on a switch port or Wi-Fi network?
o: Port-based authentication, so devices must authenticate (usually via RADIUS) before getting access
questions.e: The device is the supplicant, the switch or AP is the authenticator and RADIUS is the authentication server.

questions.q: What does network access control (NAC) do?
o: Checks devices (identity and health such as patches and antivirus) before allowing them on the network
questions.e: Non-compliant devices can be blocked or put in a remediation VLAN.

questions.q: Why is MAC filtering a weak security control on its own?
o: MAC addresses are easy to see and spoof
questions.e: Use it alongside stronger controls such as 802.1X.

questions.q: What does port security on a switch do?
