o: Limits which or how many MAC addresses can use a port, and acts when the limit is broken
questions.e: Violations can shut down the port, restrict traffic or just log.

questions.q: What is a screened subnet (DMZ)?
o: A separate network segment for public-facing servers, between the internet and the internal network
questions.e: If a public server is compromised, the attacker still can't reach the internal network directly.

questions.q: How are firewall ACL rules usually processed?
o: Top down, and the first matching rule applies, with an implicit deny at the end
questions.e: Put more specific rules above general ones.

questions.q: What does URL filtering do?
o: Blocks or allows websites based on their address or category
questions.e: Content filtering can also inspect what's on the page.

questions.q: Why is key management important?
o: Keys must be generated, stored, rotated and revoked securely, or encryption can be undermined
questions.e: Lost or stolen keys break the protection that encryption provides.

questions.q: In security zones, what is the difference between trusted and untrusted?
o: Trusted is the internal network you control; untrusted is outside it, such as the internet
questions.e: Firewalls control traffic between zones, with the screened subnet in between.

questions.q: A switch port in a public reception area isn't used. What should you do?
o: Disable it (administratively shut it down) or put it in an unused VLAN
questions.e: Unused live ports let anyone plug in.

questions.q: A new firewall rule allows HTTPS to a web server but users still can't connect. The first rule in the list denies all traffic from the internet. What is the problem?
o: Rule order: the deny rule matches first, so the allow rule is never reached
questions.e: Move the specific allow rule above the broad deny.

questions.q: Which is the most secure way to manage a switch remotely?
o: SSH with strong credentials, limited to a management network
questions.e: Combine encrypted protocols with access restrictions and logging.

questions.q: Which device should sit in the screened subnet?
questions.e: Only systems that must be reachable from the internet belong there.

questions.q: What does content filtering add beyond URL filtering?
o: It inspects the actual content of pages or files, not just the address
questions.e: For example, blocking certain file types or keywords.

questions.q: Which statement about ACLs is correct?
o: They can filter by source and destination IP, port and protocol
They only filter by MAC address
They can't be used on routers
questions.e: ACLs are used on routers, firewalls and Layer 3 switches.

questions.q: A company wants every device to prove it has up-to-date antivirus before joining the wired network. What should it deploy?
questions.e: NAC can check device health as well as identity.

questions.q: Why should default SNMP community strings be changed or SNMPv3 used?
o: Defaults like 'public' are widely known and let attackers read or change device settings
questions.e: Default credentials are one of the first things attackers try.

questions.q: What is the first step of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?
o: Establish a theory of probable cause
questions.e: Gather information, question users, identify symptoms, find out what changed and duplicate the problem if possible.

questions.q: Which step comes straight after establishing a theory of probable cause?
o: Test the theory to determine the cause
questions.e: If the test doesn't confirm the theory, set up a new theory or escalate.

questions.q: What should you do if testing doesn't confirm your theory?
o: Establish a new theory or escalate
questions.e: Don't make changes based on an unproven theory.

questions.q: What is the final step of the methodology?
o: Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned
questions.e: Documentation helps the next person who sees the same problem.

questions.q: Which step includes implementing preventive measures, if applicable?
questions.e: After fixing it, confirm everything works and take steps to stop it happening again.

questions.q: Which step includes considering multiple approaches such as top-to-bottom or bottom-to-top OSI?
o: Establish a theory of probable cause
questions.e: Divide and conquer, top-down and bottom-up are ways of working through possible causes.

questions.q: Several users report different problems at the same time. What does the methodology recommend?
o: Fix them all with one change
questions.e: Tackling problems one by one avoids confusing cause and effect.

questions.q: A user says the network 'stopped working after lunch'. What is a key question to ask during problem identification?
questions.e: Recent changes are a common cause. Check change logs too.

questions.q: What should you do before implementing a fix that could affect many users?
o: Establish a plan of action, considering the impact and change management
questions.e: Plans include rollback steps and scheduling to limit disruption.

questions.q: Which approach starts at Layer 1 and works up the OSI model?
questions.e: Bottom-up suits problems likely to be physical, such as no link light.

questions.q: Which approach starts in the middle of the OSI model, for example with a ping, then moves up or down depending on the result?
questions.e: A successful ping rules out Layers 1 to 3 quickly.

questions.q: Why try to duplicate the problem?
o: To see the symptoms for yourself and confirm what's happening
questions.e: Reproducing a fault helps confirm the cause and later the fix.

questions.q: When should you escalate a problem?
o: When it's beyond your knowledge, access or authority, or your theories have been ruled out
questions.e: Escalating follows the methodology, so don't see it as a failure.

questions.q: After applying a fix for one user, what should you do before closing the ticket?
o: Verify full system functionality with the user
questions.e: Make sure the fix worked and didn't break something else.

questions.q: Which step is 'question the obvious'?
o: Establish a theory of probable cause
questions.e: Check simple things first: is it plugged in, powered on and connected?

questions.q: Long Ethernet runs near fluorescent lights and motors show many errors. What is the likely cause?
questions.e: Re-route the cable or use shielded cable.

questions.q: What is crosstalk?
o: Signal from one wire pair bleeding into another
questions.e: Poor terminations that untwist too much wire increase crosstalk (NEXT and FEXT).

questions.q: What is attenuation?
o: Loss of signal strength over distance
questions.e: Copper and fibre both lose signal with length, which is why distance limits exist.

questions.q: Which interface counter shows frames smaller than 64 bytes?
questions.e: Runts often come from collisions or a duplex mismatch.

questions.q: Which interface counter shows frames larger than the allowed MTU?
questions.e: Giants can appear with an MTU mismatch, such as one side using jumbo frames.

questions.q: An interface shows a rising number of CRC errors. What is a likely cause?
o: A damaged cable, bad termination or interference
questions.e: CRC errors mean frames arrived corrupted, usually a physical problem.

questions.q: A switch port shows 'administratively down'. What does that mean?
o: Someone has disabled it with a shutdown command
questions.e: Enable it with 'no shutdown' if it should be in use.

questions.q: A switch port shows 'err-disabled'. What is a common reason?
o: A security feature such as port security or BPDU guard shut it down
questions.e: Fix the cause, then reset the port.

questions.q: A new access point won't power up on a PoE switch, although other APs work. What should you check?
o: Whether the switch's PoE budget is used up, and whether the AP needs PoE+ or PoE++
questions.e: Each switch has a total PoE budget, and devices need a matching PoE standard.

questions.q: Which PoE standard provides up to 30 W per port (PoE+)?
questions.e: 802.3af is about 15.4 W, 802.3at about 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 or 90 W.

questions.q: A fibre link won't come up. One end uses a single-mode transceiver and the other multimode. What is the problem?
questions.e: Transceivers, fibre type and wavelengths must match at both ends.

questions.q: A newly installed fibre link has no light. The cable is fine. What is a common simple mistake?
o: The TX and RX strands are swapped (transposed)
questions.e: TX on one end must reach RX on the other.

questions.q: A fibre link is up but with errors, and the received light level is very low. What should you check?
o: Dirty connectors, bends or damage, and whether the run is too long
questions.e: Clean connectors and check the signal strength (dB loss) against the transceiver's spec.

questions.q: A 10 Gbps link is running over Cat 5e cable for 80 metres and drops to 1 Gbps. Why?
o: Cat 5e isn't rated for 10 Gbps; Cat 6a is needed for 10 Gbps at that length
questions.e: Using the wrong cable category limits speed.

questions.q: A technician terminates a cable but untwists 5 cm of each pair. What problem might this cause?
o: Crosstalk and errors from improper termination
questions.e: Keep pairs twisted as close to the connector as possible.

questions.q: A link shows high output drops. What does that usually mean?
o: The interface is congested and its buffers are overflowing
questions.e: Drops point to more traffic than the link can carry.

questions.q: Using multimode fibre with single-mode transceivers over a long run would cause:
o: Signal problems or no link, because fibre types must match
questions.e: Always match the cable type to the transceiver.

questions.q: A port shows as 'suspended' on a link aggregation group. What is likely?
o: That member's settings don't match the bundle, so it was suspended
The cable is fine and it's forwarding
questions.e: All members need matching speed, duplex and VLAN settings.

questions.q: Which tool would quickly tell you if a copper cable has an open wire or a short?
questions.e: Cable testers check continuity and wiring order.

questions.q: Two old switches, neither supporting auto-MDIX, are connected with a straight-through cable. What happens?
o: No link, because TX and RX aren't crossed
questions.e: Use a crossover cable or a switch that supports auto-MDIX.

questions.q: Users suddenly report the whole network is extremely slow, and switch CPUs are at 100% with huge broadcast traffic. What is likely?
o: A duplex mismatch on one PC
questions.e: Loops cause broadcast storms. Check spanning tree and recent cabling changes.

questions.q: A PC in VLAN 10 is plugged into a port configured for VLAN 20. What will happen?
o: It gets the wrong subnet (or no DHCP) and can't reach its normal resources
questions.e: Check the port's VLAN assignment against the documentation.

questions.q: A user can reach local resources but nothing outside the subnet. What is a likely cause?
questions.e: Without a correct gateway, traffic can't leave the subnet.

questions.q: Users can reach sites by IP address but not by name. What is likely?
questions.e: Check the DNS server settings and whether the server responds.

questions.q: New devices are getting APIPA addresses while existing ones work. What is a likely cause?
o: The DHCP scope has run out of addresses (pool exhaustion)
questions.e: Shorten the lease time, enlarge the scope or tidy up old leases.

questions.q: A PC shows a 'duplicate IP address' warning. What has happened?
o: Another device is already using the same IP, often due to a static address inside the DHCP range
questions.e: Exclude static addresses from the DHCP scope.

questions.q: A user has IP 192.168.1.50 with mask 255.255.0.0 while everyone else uses 255.255.255.0. What problem might this cause?
o: Wrong subnet mask, so the PC misjudges which hosts are local
questions.e: The /16 mask makes the PC treat any 192.168.x.x host as local, so it ARPs for them instead of sending traffic to the gateway.

questions.q: Traffic to a server is blocked after a firewall change, but only for one subnet. What should you check first?
o: The ACL rules added in the change
questions.e: Misconfigured ACLs often block more than intended.

questions.q: A router can't reach the internet, and 'show ip route' shows no 0.0.0.0/0 entry. What is missing?
questions.e: Without a default route, packets for unknown networks are dropped.

questions.q: Why might the wrong switch become the STP root bridge?
o: The priority wasn't set, so an old switch with a lower MAC address won the election
questions.e: Set the root priority deliberately on a core switch.

questions.q: Which STP port role is the best path towards the root bridge on a non-root switch?
questions.e: Each non-root switch has one root port. Designated ports forward away from the root.

questions.q: Wi-Fi users drop off when walking between two APs. What could cause this?
o: Poor roaming due to coverage gaps or AP settings
questions.e: Check overlap between APs, signal strength and roaming features.

questions.q: Neighbouring APs are all on channel 1 and users report slow Wi-Fi. What is the issue?
questions.e: Spread APs across 1, 6 and 11 on 2.4 GHz, or use 5 GHz.

questions.q: Users far from an AP get a weak signal and slow speeds. What is this?
o: Signal loss due to distance and obstacles
questions.e: Add APs, reposition them or change antennas based on a site survey.

questions.q: A client keeps disconnecting from Wi-Fi without moving. What should you investigate?
o: Interference, signal strength and disassociation events, including possible deauthentication attacks
questions.e: Disassociation can be caused by interference, AP settings or an attacker.

questions.q: Microwave ovens in the staff kitchen disrupt Wi-Fi at lunch. Which band is affected?
questions.e: Microwaves operate around 2.4 GHz. Moving clients to 5 GHz helps.

questions.q: A switch port has the wrong native VLAN on one end of a trunk. What may happen?
o: Untagged traffic leaks into the wrong VLAN and CDP/LLDP may log a native VLAN mismatch
questions.e: Native VLANs must match on both ends of a trunk.

questions.q: Wi-Fi works but a site visitor can't reach the internet on guest Wi-Fi until they open a browser. Why?
o: A captive portal needs them to accept terms or log in first
questions.e: Captive portals intercept the first web request.

questions.q: What is a common fix for DHCP address pool exhaustion on a busy guest network?
o: Reduce the lease time and/or enlarge the scope
Increase the lease time to 30 days
questions.e: Short leases free addresses from devices that have left.

questions.q: Two routers keep passing packets back and forth for one destination, and traceroute shows the same hops repeating. What is this?
questions.e: Check static routes and routing protocol configuration. TTL eventually drops the packets.

questions.q: Which STP port state forwards traffic normally?
questions.e: Ports pass through listening and learning before forwarding in classic STP.

questions.q: What is jitter?
o: Variation in packet delay, which makes voice and video choppy
questions.e: QoS and enough bandwidth help keep jitter low.

questions.q: What is latency?
o: The time it takes data to travel from source to destination
questions.e: High latency makes interactive applications feel slow.

questions.q: What is the difference between bandwidth and throughput?
o: Bandwidth is the link's capacity; throughput is the data actually delivered
questions.e: Throughput is lower due to overhead, congestion and errors.

questions.q: What is a bottleneck?
o: The slowest point in a path that limits overall performance
questions.e: For example, a 1 Gbps uplink serving many 1 Gbps users.

questions.q: Many users share a single 1 Gbps uplink and it runs at 100% at peak times. What is this?
questions.e: Upgrade the link, add link aggregation or apply QoS.

questions.q: Video calls freeze and have missing sound. Monitoring shows 5% packet loss. What should you look at?
o: Packet loss causes, such as congestion, errors on a link or Wi-Fi interference
questions.e: Real-time apps cope badly with even small amounts of loss.

questions.q: Which is most sensitive to jitter and latency?
questions.e: Interactive real-time traffic needs consistent, low delay.

questions.q: A satellite link has high latency even when lightly used. Why?
o: The signal travels a very long distance to and from the satellite
questions.e: Geostationary satellites add hundreds of milliseconds of delay.

questions.q: A file transfer is slow on a 1 Gbps link. Interface counters show many CRC errors. What is the likely cause of poor throughput?
questions.e: Errors mean resending data, which cuts throughput.

questions.q: Which tool helps confirm the actual throughput a user is getting?
o: A speed tester or throughput test tool
questions.e: Compare results against expected speeds and baselines.

questions.q: Which technique prioritises VoIP during congestion?
questions.e: QoS marks and queues traffic so time-sensitive packets go first.

questions.q: A Wi-Fi network slows when 60 people join a meeting room AP at once. What is the main cause?
o: Too many clients contending for the same AP's airtime
questions.e: Add APs for high-density areas and use 5 or 6 GHz.

questions.q: Why is device uptime a useful performance metric?
o: It shows reliability and whether a device has restarted unexpectedly
questions.e: Unexpected reboots can explain intermittent problems.

questions.q: Users on public hotspot Wi-Fi get slow speeds and pages that won't load until they log in. What explains the login part?
o: The hotspot uses a captive portal
questions.e: Until the portal is completed, most traffic is blocked or redirected.

questions.q: What does packet loss mean?
o: Some packets never arrive at their destination
questions.e: Causes include congestion, errors and interference.

questions.q: Which command tests basic reachability to another host?
questions.e: Ping sends ICMP echo requests. No reply doesn't always mean the host is down, as ICMP may be blocked.

questions.q: Which command shows each router hop on the path to a destination on Windows?
questions.e: Windows uses tracert. Linux and macOS use traceroute.

questions.q: Which tools query DNS records directly?
questions.e: dig is common on Linux and macOS. nslookup is on Windows and Linux.

questions.q: Which command shows active connections and listening ports on a computer?
questions.e: Useful for spotting unexpected services or connections.

questions.q: Which command shows the IP configuration on a Windows PC?
questions.e: Linux uses 'ip addr' (or the older ifconfig).

questions.q: Which command shows the IP to MAC address mappings a computer has learned?
questions.e: Useful for spotting duplicate IPs or ARP spoofing.

questions.q: What does Nmap do?
o: Scans hosts to find open ports, services and sometimes operating systems
questions.e: Only scan networks you're authorised to test.

questions.q: What does tcpdump do?
o: Captures packets from the command line, usually on Linux
questions.e: Captures can be opened in a protocol analyser such as Wireshark.

questions.q: What is a protocol analyser such as Wireshark used for?
o: Capturing and decoding network traffic to see exactly what's happening
questions.e: It shows each packet's headers and contents.

questions.q: What do LLDP and CDP show?
o: Information about directly connected neighbouring devices, such as their name, port and model
questions.e: LLDP is the open standard. CDP is Cisco's protocol.

questions.q: Which hardware tool finds which wall jack a cable in a bundle connects to?
questions.e: The toner puts a signal on the cable and the probe picks it up at the other end.

questions.q: Which tool shines visible red light down a fibre to find breaks or sharp bends?
questions.e: Light escapes at the fault and can be seen.

questions.q: Which tool shows nearby wireless networks, channels and signal strengths?
questions.e: Use it to pick clear channels and find interference.

questions.q: What is a network tap?
o: A hardware device that copies traffic from a link for monitoring
questions.e: Taps give a full copy of traffic, unlike some mirror ports that may drop frames under load.

questions.q: Which switch command shows which MAC addresses have been learned on which ports?
questions.e: Useful for finding which port a device is plugged into. Older IOS versions and the objectives write it as show mac-address-table.

questions.q: Which switch command shows each port's VLAN membership?
questions.e: Check this when a device is on the wrong network.

questions.q: Which device command shows PoE power use per port?
questions.e: Helps diagnose PoE budget problems.

questions.q: Which command shows a device's interface status, errors and counters?
questions.e: Look for errors, drops, duplex and speed.

questions.q: Which command displays a device's running configuration?
questions.e: Compare it with the saved and golden configs.

questions.q: A user can't reach a server. Ping by IP works but nslookup fails. What should you check?
questions.e: Ping working rules out basic connectivity.

questions.q: Which Linux command shows interface addresses on modern systems?
questions.e: ifconfig is older and may not be installed by default.

questions.q: Which hardware tool checks whether a wired cable meets its rated performance, such as for Cat 6?
questions.e: Basic testers check wiring. Certifiers test performance against the standard.

questions.q: A traceroute stops responding after the third hop. What does this suggest?
o: A problem at or after that hop, or a device there blocking ICMP
questions.e: Some routers don't reply to traceroute, so check further before assuming a fault.

questions.q: Which tool shows a device's route table on Windows?
questions.e: Linux uses 'ip route' or 'route -n'.

questions.q: What is the PDU called at the Data Link layer?
questions.e: Layer 2 wraps each packet in a frame with source and destination MAC addresses and a trailer for error checking.

questions.q: Which sequence describes the TCP three-way handshake?
questions.e: The client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK and the client confirms with ACK. Only then does data flow. This happens at Layer 4.

questions.q: A switch keeps sending frames for a PC out of the port the PC used to be plugged into, because its MAC table holds an old entry. Which OSI layer is the problem at?
questions.e: MAC address tables and frame forwarding are Layer 2 functions. The entry will age out, or you can clear it.

questions.q: Which OSI layers does a network interface card (NIC) work at?
questions.e: A NIC puts signals on the medium (Layer 1) and has a MAC address and builds frames (Layer 2).

questions.q: Which TCP/IP (DoD) model layer lines up with OSI Layer 3?
questions.e: The Internet layer handles IP addressing and routing, the same job as the OSI Network layer.

questions.q: Which part of an Ethernet frame holds the value used to check it arrived without errors?
o: The frame check sequence (FCS) in the trailer
questions.e: The sender calculates a CRC and places it in the FCS. The receiver recalculates it, and a mismatch means the frame is dropped.

questions.q: A firewall rule blocks TCP port 443. Which OSI layer's information is the rule matching on?
questions.e: Port numbers live in the TCP and UDP headers, which are Layer 4.

questions.q: How does a reverse proxy differ from a forward proxy?
o: A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and handles requests coming in from clients on the internet
A reverse proxy only works for email
A reverse proxy assigns IP addresses to clients
questions.e: A forward proxy acts for internal clients going out. A reverse proxy acts for servers, handling inbound requests and often doing TLS offload, caching and load balancing.

questions.q: What does a next-generation firewall (NGFW) add over a basic packet-filtering firewall?
o: Application awareness and deep packet inspection, often with built-in IPS
The ability to work without rules
questions.e: An NGFW can identify applications regardless of port, inspect content and block threats, not just match IPs and ports.

questions.q: What does a stateful firewall do that a stateless one doesn't?
o: Tracks connections, so return traffic for a connection started inside is allowed automatically
Checks each packet with no memory of earlier packets
Blocks all inbound traffic with no exceptions
questions.e: Stateful firewalls keep a state table of active sessions. Stateless filters judge each packet on its own against the rules.

questions.q: How does a load balancer know to stop sending traffic to a server that has failed?
questions.e: The load balancer regularly probes each server (for example, requesting a web page) and takes any that fail out of the pool.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a virtual firewall appliance over a physical one?
o: It can be deployed, copied and scaled quickly with no new hardware
It works without a hypervisor or host
questions.e: Virtual appliances run as VMs, so they're quick to spin up, snapshot and scale, which suits cloud and virtualised networks.

questions.q: Which field in the IP header is commonly used to mark packets for QoS?
questions.e: Devices mark packets with a DSCP value, and routers and switches along the path use it to decide which traffic goes first.

questions.q: What is the job of a VPN concentrator (VPN headend)?
o: Terminating many VPN tunnels from remote users or sites in one place
questions.e: A concentrator handles the encryption and authentication for large numbers of VPN connections.

questions.q: A company wants traffic to keep flowing if its inline IPS fails, even though that means no inspection. What is this setting called?
questions.e: Fail-open keeps the network up when the device fails. Fail-closed blocks traffic, protecting security at the cost of availability.

questions.q: What is VPC peering?
o: A private connection between two VPCs so they can route to each other using private addresses
A VPN to a home user
Two clouds sharing one public IP
questions.e: Peering lets resources in separate VPCs talk without going over the internet.

questions.q: In a VPC, what makes a subnet public?
o: Its route table has a route to an internet gateway
questions.e: Subnets are public or private by routing. A route to an internet gateway lets resources with public IPs reach and be reached from the internet.

questions.q: Which cloud connectivity option is quickest and cheapest to set up, but runs over the public internet?
questions.e: A VPN uses existing internet links with encryption. Direct Connect-style links are private and more consistent but take longer to set up and cost more.

questions.q: Which deployment model gives an organisation the most control, with cloud infrastructure used only by that organisation?
questions.e: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation, either on site or hosted.

questions.q: A retailer's website gets ten times its normal traffic on Black Friday, then returns to normal. Which cloud feature lets it add capacity for the day and give it back afterwards?
questions.e: Elasticity adds and removes resources automatically as demand changes, so the retailer only pays for the extra capacity while it's used.

questions.q: Who manages the operating system in the IaaS model?
o: Nobody, as IaaS has no operating system
questions.e: In IaaS the provider runs the hardware, storage and virtualisation. The customer installs, patches and secures the OS and everything above it.

questions.q: What is a risk of multitenancy that cloud providers must control?
o: One customer's data or traffic being exposed to another customer on the same hardware
Customers running out of IP addresses
questions.e: Tenants share infrastructure, so strong logical isolation is essential.

questions.q: In general, how do cloud security groups differ from network security lists?
o: Security groups apply to individual instances or interfaces; security lists apply to a whole subnet
Security groups only work with IPv6
Security lists encrypt data and security groups don't
They are both types of VPN
questions.e: Both filter traffic. The difference is scope: per instance (or interface) versus per subnet.

questions.q: Which connector is used on Cat 6 Ethernet patch cables?
questions.e: RJ45 (8P8C) has eight pins for the four twisted pairs. RJ11 is the smaller telephone connector.

questions.q: Which fibre connector is square, uses a push-pull latch and is about twice the size of LC?
questions.e: SC is the older full-size push-pull connector. LC is the small form factor version.

questions.q: Besides Ethernet, which protocol are SFP and QSFP transceivers commonly made for?
questions.e: Transceivers are protocol specific. Fibre Channel ones are used for storage area networks.

questions.q: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite internet services improve on older satellite services mainly by offering:
o: Much lower latency, as the satellites are far closer to Earth
questions.e: Older geostationary satellites are around 36,000 km up, giving latency of 600 ms or more. LEO satellites orbit a few hundred kilometres up.

questions.q: How many links are needed to fully mesh five sites?
questions.e: A full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links. For five sites that's 5 x 4 / 2 = 10.

questions.q: In a spine-and-leaf data centre, what do servers connect to?
questions.e: Servers and storage plug into leaf (top-of-rack) switches. Leaves connect up to every spine.

questions.q: A small business in one building wants the benefits of a tiered design without paying for three layers of switches. What should it use?
o: A collapsed core, with core and distribution combined
A full mesh of every switch
questions.e: Collapsing core and distribution into one layer cuts cost and suits smaller sites.

questions.q: A server copies a nightly backup to another server in the same data centre. Which traffic flow is this?
questions.e: East-west is traffic between devices inside the data centre. North-south enters or leaves it.

questions.q: Which three-tier layer should avoid heavy packet filtering so it can move traffic as fast as possible?
questions.e: The core's job is fast, reliable transport. Policy and filtering belong at distribution.

questions.q: A spine-and-leaf data centre needs more server ports. What is the usual way to add them?
o: Add another leaf switch and connect it to every spine
Connect a new switch to one existing leaf
Add a link between two leaves
questions.e: Scaling out is simple: each new leaf connects to all spines, keeping the same hop count between any two servers.

questions.q: In the three-tier model, where is PoE for phones and access points usually provided?
questions.e: End devices plug into access switches, so that's where PoE ports are needed.

questions.q: Every branch office connects only to head office, and branch-to-branch traffic goes through head office. Which topology is this?
questions.e: Hub-and-spoke is cheap and simple to manage, but the hub is a single point of failure and branch-to-branch traffic takes the long way round.

questions.q: What is the main downside of a full mesh?
o: The number of links, and so the cost and complexity, grows quickly with each new node
Every link is a single point of failure
questions.e: Each new node needs a link to every other node, so full mesh is usually kept to small numbers of critical sites or devices.

questions.q: Which traffic flow does a perimeter firewall mainly inspect?
questions.e: The perimeter sits between the inside and the internet, so it sees traffic entering and leaving. East-west needs internal segmentation.

questions.q: What is 255.255.255.240 in CIDR notation?
questions.e: 240 is 11110000, so four extra bits on top of 24 makes /28: 16 addresses, 14 usable.

questions.q: Which address class is reserved for experimental use?
questions.e: Class E is reserved and not used for normal hosts. Class D is multicast.

questions.q: What is zero-touch provisioning in SD-WAN?
o: A new branch device downloads its configuration automatically when it's plugged in
Engineers configure each device by hand on site
Users set up their own WAN links
questions.e: Zero-touch means someone on site only needs to cable and power the device. The controller sends it everything else.

questions.q: What does it mean that SD-WAN is transport agnostic?
o: It can use any link type, such as broadband, MPLS or 4G/5G, and treat them as one pool
questions.e: SD-WAN builds overlays across whatever links are available and picks the best one for each application.

questions.q: What is configuration drift?
o: Devices' configurations slowly changing away from the approved baseline
Wireless clients moving between access points
questions.e: Manual one-off changes build up over time. IaC tools can spot drift and put devices back to the defined state.

questions.q: In source control, what is a branch used for?
o: Working on a change separately without affecting the main version until it's reviewed and merged
questions.e: Branches let several people work in parallel. Conflicts are spotted when changes are merged.

questions.q: Why does VXLAN suit large data centres better than standard VLANs?
o: Its 24-bit network identifier allows about 16 million segments, compared with about 4,000 VLANs
It needs no IP network underneath
It removes the need for switches
questions.e: VLAN IDs are 12 bits (up to 4,094 usable). VXLAN's VNI is 24 bits, which suits multitenant data centres.

questions.q: What does it mean that SD-WAN is application aware?
o: It recognises applications and sends each over the best link according to policy
It installs applications on users' PCs
It blocks all applications by default
questions.e: For example, voice can be sent over the link with the lowest jitter while bulk backups use a cheaper link.

questions.q: What is the default administrative distance of OSPF on Cisco devices?
questions.e: Common defaults: connected 0, static 1, EIGRP internal 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120, external BGP 20.

questions.q: In OSPF, what are areas used for, with area 0 as the backbone?
o: Grouping routers to keep link-state databases smaller and limit how far changes spread
questions.e: All other areas must connect to area 0. Splitting a big network into areas reduces the work each router does.

questions.q: A router learns the same network from OSPF (AD 110) and from internal EIGRP (AD 90). Which route goes in the routing table?
o: The EIGRP route, because its administrative distance is lower
The OSPF route, because 110 is higher
questions.e: When prefix lengths match, the lower AD wins. Metrics are only compared between routes from the same source.

questions.q: What is router-on-a-stick?
o: One router interface split into subinterfaces, one per VLAN, over a trunk link for inter-VLAN routing
A wireless router on a pole
A backup router that only runs during outages
questions.e: Each subinterface gets an 802.1Q VLAN tag and an IP that acts as that VLAN's gateway.

questions.q: In BGP, what does an autonomous system number (ASN) identify?
o: A network under one organisation's control, such as an ISP
questions.e: BGP routes between autonomous systems, and the AS path is a key part of how it chooses routes.

questions.q: On a Cisco switch, which commands create VLAN 30 and name it Sales?
questions.e: In global configuration mode, vlan 30 enters VLAN configuration, and name Sales sets its name.

questions.q: Which range of VLAN IDs can be used with 802.1Q?
questions.e: The VLAN ID field is 12 bits. IDs 0 and 4095 are reserved, leaving 1 to 4094.

questions.q: A storage team enables jumbo frames on its servers, but transfers fail. What should be checked?
o: That every switch port and device along the path is set to the same larger MTU
That the servers have IPv6 enabled
questions.e: A device still set to 1500 bytes will drop larger frames. Jumbo frames must match end to end.

questions.q: Which STP port state learns MAC addresses but doesn't yet forward user frames?
questions.e: Classic STP goes blocking, listening, learning, then forwarding, which is why it can take 30 to 50 seconds for a port to come up.

questions.q: Both ends of a link are set to auto speed and duplex. What happens?
o: They negotiate the best speed and duplex they both support
They default to 10 Mbps half duplex
They use whichever end booted first
questions.e: Auto-negotiation works best when both ends use it. Problems usually start when one end is hard-set and the other is on auto.

questions.q: Which wireless network type has clients connecting through an access point?
questions.e: Infrastructure mode is the normal office and home setup. Ad hoc connects devices directly with no AP.

questions.q: What do WPA2-Enterprise and WPA3-Enterprise use to authenticate each user?
questions.e: Each user signs in with their own credentials or certificate, checked by an authentication server.

questions.q: How does an autonomous access point differ from a lightweight one?
o: It's configured and managed on its own, without needing a wireless LAN controller
It must be powered by a battery
questions.e: Autonomous APs suit small sites. Lightweight APs rely on a controller, which suits larger deployments.

questions.q: Which 802.11 standard is Wi-Fi 5?
questions.e: Wi-Fi 4 is 802.11n, Wi-Fi 5 is 802.11ac (5 GHz) and Wi-Fi 6/6E is 802.11ax.

questions.q: What temperature range is usually recommended for server and network rooms?
o: Any temperature, as long as it's dry
questions.e: ASHRAE guidance for equipment intake air is roughly 18 to 27 °C. Too hot shortens equipment life. Too cold wastes energy and can cause condensation.

questions.q: A switch is described as port-side exhaust. How should it be mounted in a rack with hot and cold aisles?
o: With its ports facing the hot aisle, as hot air leaves from the port side
With its ports facing the cold aisle
questions.e: Port-side exhaust means air comes in at the back and leaves at the front, where the ports are. The intake side must face the cold aisle.

questions.q: A 42U rack holds a 1U patch panel, a 1U switch and a 2U UPS. How much space is left?
questions.e: 1 + 1 + 2 = 4U used, so 42 - 4 = 38U remain.

questions.q: Why is a generator often installed alongside a UPS?
o: The UPS covers the few seconds or minutes until the generator starts and takes over for longer outages
The generator charges the UPS during normal use
A UPS can't run without a generator
questions.e: UPS batteries only last a short time. The generator provides long-term power.

questions.q: What is the standard mains voltage in the UK?
questions.e: UK mains is nominally 230 V AC at 50 Hz. Kit should be rated for it, and PDUs must match the supply.

questions.q: A new office floor needs 40 network points, and the MDF is three floors down. Where would the access switches normally go?
o: In an IDF on that floor, linked back to the MDF
In the MDF, with 40 cables run down three floors
questions.e: IDFs keep copper runs short (under 100 m) and connect back to the MDF over backbone cabling, often fibre.

questions.q: Why should network cables be labelled at both ends?
o: So technicians can trace and change connections quickly without unplugging the wrong one
So they don't need a patch panel
questions.e: Clear labelling matched to documentation saves time and avoids outages.

questions.q: What is a pre-action sprinkler system?
o: Pipes stay dry until a detector triggers, and water only flows if a sprinkler head also opens
Pipes are always full of water
It sprays gas instead of water
It only works in cold rooms
questions.e: The two-stage design cuts the risk of accidental water damage in rooms full of equipment.

questions.q: What are blanking panels for in a rack?
o: Filling empty spaces so hot exhaust air can't loop back to the front of the equipment
questions.e: Gaps let hot air recirculate to the cold side, which raises intake temperatures.

questions.q: Equipment in a rack draws 1,200 W on a 230 V supply. Roughly how much current is that?
questions.e: Current = power / voltage, so 1,200 / 230 is about 5.2 A. Use this to check the load against the circuit and PDU ratings.

questions.q: Why keep power cables and copper data cables apart in trays and racks?
o: To reduce electromagnetic interference on the data cables
To allow more airflow to the UPS
questions.e: Running data cables alongside mains cables can induce noise and cause errors.

questions.q: Why does an asset inventory record warranty and support dates?
o: To know what's covered for repairs and to plan replacements before support ends
questions.e: Warranty and support details tell you who to call and when kit needs renewing.

questions.q: What should a Layer 2 network diagram show?
o: Switches, VLANs, trunks and how devices connect at the data link level
questions.e: Layer 2 diagrams help with VLAN, trunking and spanning tree problems. Layer 3 diagrams show subnets and routing.

questions.q: Why track software licences in the asset inventory?
o: To stay compliant, avoid using more copies than you've paid for and know when renewals are due
questions.e: Licensing is part of asset management alongside hardware, warranties and support.

questions.q: When should a wireless site survey be carried out?
o: Before installing a wireless network and after major changes to the building or layout
Never, if the APs are new
questions.e: A survey shows where APs should go and confirms coverage afterwards. The result is usually shown as a heat map.

questions.q: A change has caused an outage. Which part of the approved change request should the engineer follow?
questions.e: Every change should include a tested way to undo it if things go wrong.

questions.q: An SLA promises 99.9% uptime. Roughly how much downtime does that allow in a year?
questions.e: 0.1% of 8,760 hours is about 8.76 hours. 99.99% would allow only about 53 minutes.

questions.q: On a Cisco device, what is the difference between the running configuration and the startup configuration?
o: The running config is the live one in RAM; the startup config is saved in NVRAM and loaded at boot
The startup config is only used for routing
The running config is stored on a USB stick
questions.e: Changes take effect in the running config straight away but are lost on reboot unless saved with copy running-config startup-config.

questions.q: Why compare device configurations with the golden configuration regularly?
o: To spot unauthorised changes and drift from the approved baseline
To make the devices run faster
questions.e: Configuration monitoring flags differences so they can be checked and corrected.

questions.q: What is a change advisory board (CAB)?
o: A group that reviews, approves or rejects proposed changes
The team that writes the SLA
questions.e: The CAB weighs up risk, timing and impact before a change goes ahead.

questions.q: Which UDP port do SNMP traps normally use?
questions.e: Managers poll agents on UDP 161. Agents send traps to the manager on UDP 162.

questions.q: What is an SNMP OID?
o: A unique identifier for one value an agent can report, such as an interface's input errors
The name of the SNMP manager
questions.e: OIDs are arranged in a tree and described by the MIB.

questions.q: What is the difference between SNMP polling and SNMP traps?
o: With polling the manager asks the agent for data; with traps the agent sends an alert as soon as something happens
Polling is encrypted and traps aren't
questions.e: Polling gives regular readings for graphs. Traps give fast alerts for events like an interface going down.

questions.q: Which syslog severity level is the most serious?
questions.e: Syslog runs from 0 (Emergency) to 7 (Debug). Lower numbers are more severe.

questions.q: What does syslog severity level 7 mean?
questions.e: Debug messages are very detailed and normally only turned on while troubleshooting.

questions.q: What is ad hoc network discovery?
o: A one-off scan run when needed, for example after an incident or a change
A scan that runs every hour automatically
Discovering networks with no IP addresses
questions.e: Scheduled discovery runs regularly. Ad hoc discovery is run on demand.

questions.q: A SIEM raises an alert because one account logged in from London and then from Sydney ten minutes later. What is it doing?
o: Correlating events and flagging an anomaly
questions.e: SIEMs pull logs from many sources and look for patterns that don't fit, such as impossible travel.

questions.q: Which port does syslog use by default?
questions.e: Standard syslog uses UDP 514. Secure syslog over TLS commonly uses TCP 6514.

questions.q: Why might a port mirror miss traffic on a busy network?
o: The mirrored traffic can exceed the speed of the port it's copied to, so the switch drops some of it
questions.e: If you mirror several busy ports to one, the destination can be oversubscribed. A hardware tap doesn't have this problem.

questions.q: For availability, is a higher or lower MTBF better?
o: Higher, as the device runs longer between failures
Lower, as failures are fixed faster
It depends on the cable type
questions.e: MTBF measures reliability. MTTR measures how quickly things are fixed, and lower is better there.

questions.q: A pair of firewalls has one unit handling all traffic while the other waits to take over. Which HA approach is this?
questions.e: The standby unit takes over if the active one fails. Active-active shares the load between both.

questions.q: A business sets an RPO of one hour but only backs up once a day. What is the problem?
o: It could lose up to 24 hours of data, far more than the one hour allowed
The backups will be too large
questions.e: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss. Backups (or replication) must run at least as often as the RPO.

questions.q: What does a falling MTTR show?
questions.e: Lower mean time to repair means shorter outages and better availability.

questions.q: Why is a tabletop exercise useful?
o: It finds gaps in the DR plan cheaply, with no risk to live systems
It proves the backups definitely work
It replaces the need for any other testing
It moves systems to the DR site
questions.e: People talk through a scenario step by step. It doesn't test the technology itself, so validation tests are still needed.

questions.q: Two servers run active-active, each at 70% load. One fails. What is the likely result?
o: The remaining server can't carry the full load, so performance suffers
questions.e: For active-active to survive a failure cleanly, each node should normally run at under 50% so one can carry everything.

questions.q: How does the RTO affect the choice of recovery site?
o: A shorter RTO needs a hotter site, which costs more
A shorter RTO means a cold site is best
RTO has nothing to do with site choice
A longer RTO needs a hot site
questions.e: If you must be back within minutes, you need a hot site. If days are acceptable, a cold site may do.

questions.q: Why should DR plans be tested regularly?
o: Systems, staff and suppliers change, and an untested plan often fails when it's needed
questions.e: Regular testing keeps contact lists, steps and recovery times accurate.

questions.q: A switch has an MTBF of 200,000 hours. What does that mean?
o: On average, units of that model run about 200,000 hours between failures; it isn't a guarantee for any single unit
It will definitely fail at 200,000 hours
It will take 200,000 hours to repair
It must be replaced every 200,000 hours
questions.e: MTBF is a statistical average across many units.

questions.q: Why do some businesses use a cloud provider as their DR site?
o: Resources can be started quickly when needed and paid for mainly when used
It removes the need for backups
questions.e: Cloud DR avoids paying for a second data centre that sits idle, though it still needs planning and testing.

questions.q: Which DR site suits a business that can cope with being down for several days and wants the lowest cost?
questions.e: A cold site provides space, power and connectivity, but equipment and data must be brought in.

questions.q: What are the four steps of getting a DHCP lease, in order?
questions.e: Remember DORA. The client broadcasts Discover, servers Offer, the client Requests one offer and that server Acknowledges.

questions.q: Which DNS zone type resolves IP addresses to names?
questions.e: Reverse zones hold PTR records. Forward zones map names to addresses.

questions.q: Which DNS record maps a name to an IPv4 address?
questions.e: A is IPv4. AAAA (quad A) is IPv6.

questions.q: Which ports does DHCP use?
o: UDP 67 on the server and UDP 68 on the client
questions.e: DHCP runs over UDP, as clients start with no IP address and rely on broadcasts.

questions.q: A remote worker on a split-tunnel VPN watches a video on a public website. Where does that traffic go?
o: Straight out through their home internet connection, not through the VPN
Through the VPN to the company first
Through the company's DNS server only
questions.e: Split tunnelling only sends company-bound traffic through the tunnel, which saves company bandwidth but means less control over the rest.

questions.q: What is a downside of a full-tunnel VPN?
o: All of the user's traffic uses the company's connection, adding load and often slowing browsing
questions.e: The trade-off for full visibility and control is extra load on the company's internet link and VPN gateway.

questions.q: What do you usually need to make a console connection to a switch from a modern laptop?
o: A USB-to-serial console cable and a terminal emulator such as PuTTY
A crossover Ethernet cable and a web browser
questions.e: Laptops rarely have serial ports, so a USB console cable (or a USB console port on the device) is used.

questions.q: What is the usual default console speed on Cisco devices?
questions.e: The common settings are 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit and no flow control.

questions.q: Which protocol suite is most often used to build site-to-site VPN tunnels?
questions.e: IPsec provides encryption (ESP), authentication and key exchange (IKE) between the two sites' gateways.

questions.q: Why should device management interfaces sit on a separate management VLAN?
o: So only authorised admin systems can reach them, away from user traffic
Because SSH doesn't work on other VLANs
questions.e: Separating management traffic limits who can even try to log in to network devices.

questions.q: An engineer needs to apply the same NTP setting to 200 switches. Which method suits best?
o: Using the devices' API or an automation tool
Logging in to each switch's GUI one at a time
Connecting a console cable to each switch
questions.e: APIs and automation make repeatable changes quickly and consistently across many devices.

questions.q: Which is a common out-of-band option for a remote site?
o: A console server reached through a separate 4G/5G connection
SSH over the site's main internet link
A web GUI on the production network
A clientless VPN through the main firewall
questions.e: If the main network or firewall is down, the separate path still reaches the devices' console ports.

questions.q: Why should a jump box enforce MFA and log every session?
o: It's a gateway to sensitive systems, so it's a high-value target and needs a clear audit trail
questions.e: A compromised jump box can give an attacker a route to everything it manages.

questions.q: What is a downside of managing many devices through their web GUIs?
o: It's slow and manual, so mistakes and inconsistencies creep in at scale
GUIs can't be secured with HTTPS
GUIs only work on the console port
questions.e: GUIs are fine for one-off tasks, but scripting or APIs are better for repeated changes.

questions.q: In a site-to-site VPN, do users' PCs need VPN client software?
o: No, the routers or firewalls at each site handle the tunnel
Yes, every PC needs a client
questions.e: Site-to-site VPNs are transparent to users. Client-to-site VPNs need a client (or a browser, for clientless).

questions.q: What is a honeynet?
o: A network of honeypots set up to study attackers' behaviour
questions.e: A honeynet looks like a real environment, so it can show how attackers move between systems.

questions.q: In security terms, what is risk?
o: The likelihood that a threat will exploit a vulnerability, combined with the impact if it does
questions.e: Risk weighs how likely something is against how much damage it would do.

questions.q: What is the difference between a threat and a vulnerability?
o: A threat is something that could cause harm; a vulnerability is a weakness it could use
A vulnerability is always a person
A threat is a type of patch
questions.e: For example, a ransomware group is a threat, and an unpatched VPN appliance is a vulnerability.

questions.q: Why put staff-owned (BYOD) devices on a separate network segment?
o: The company can't fully control their security, so segmenting limits the damage if one is compromised
So they can reach every server directly
questions.e: BYOD devices often get their own VLAN or SSID with access only to what they need.

questions.q: What is LDAP used for?
o: Querying and managing a directory of users, groups and devices, such as Active Directory
questions.e: LDAP uses TCP 389, or 636 for LDAPS, which is LDAP over TLS.

questions.q: What is the difference between a rogue access point and an evil twin?
o: A rogue AP is any unauthorised AP on the network; an evil twin copies a real network's SSID to trick users into joining
An evil twin is always wired
A rogue AP only works on 6 GHz
questions.e: A rogue AP is often added innocently by staff. An evil twin is deliberately set up by an attacker.

questions.q: Users start seeing certificate warnings on websites that normally work fine. Which attack should you suspect?
o: An on-path attack intercepting HTTPS traffic
questions.e: An attacker in the middle can't present the real site's certificate, so browsers warn. Users should be told not to click through.

questions.q: What is vishing?
o: A virus in an email attachment
questions.e: Attackers pose as banks or IT support on calls to get passwords or codes. Smishing is the text message version.

questions.q: Which defence helps most against a large DDoS on a public website?
o: A cloud-based DDoS protection service or CDN that absorbs and filters the traffic upstream
questions.e: Big floods overwhelm on-site links, so they're best stopped before they reach your connection.

questions.q: Which malware type pretends to be legitimate software so users install it?
questions.e: Trojans rely on tricking the user. Worms spread by themselves.

questions.q: A switch suddenly floods all traffic out of every port, and a new laptop is generating thousands of fake MAC addresses. Which attack is this?
questions.e: Once the MAC table is full the switch floods frames, letting the attacker capture traffic. Port security limits MACs per port.

questions.q: What is an implicit deny?
o: The hidden rule at the end of an ACL that blocks anything not explicitly allowed
A rule added by an IPS
questions.e: If no rule matches, the traffic is dropped. That's why you must explicitly permit what you need.

questions.q: Which hardening step should be done on every new network device before it goes live?
o: Change the default username and password
questions.e: Default credentials are published online and are one of the first things attackers try.

questions.q: In 802.1X, what role does the switch or access point play?
questions.e: The supplicant is the client, the authenticator is the switch or AP, and the authentication server is usually RADIUS.

questions.q: A port has port security set to one MAC address with the shutdown violation mode. A user plugs a small switch in and connects two PCs. What happens?
o: The port goes into an err-disabled state
questions.e: A second MAC triggers a violation and the port shuts down until an admin clears it.

questions.q: Why disable unused services such as Telnet and the HTTP web interface on a router?
o: Each running service is another way in, so turning them off reduces the attack surface
questions.e: Keep only what you need, and use secure versions such as SSH and HTTPS.

questions.q: An ACL's first line is 'deny any any' and its second line permits HTTPS to a web server. What happens to HTTPS traffic to that server?
o: It's blocked, because the first matching line wins
It's allowed, because the permit is more specific
The ACL is rejected by the router
questions.e: ACLs are read top down and stop at the first match, so order matters. Specific permits must come before broad denies.

questions.q: Where should specific rules go in an ACL?
o: In a separate ACL on another router
questions.e: Because processing stops at the first match, a broad rule placed first would hide the specific ones beneath it.

questions.q: An administrator who had access to the VPN's pre-shared keys leaves the company. What should happen, as part of key management?
o: Change (rotate) the keys they had access to
Nothing, as keys never need changing
Write the keys on the rack door
questions.e: Keys should be rotated when people leave, on a schedule, and whenever compromise is suspected.

questions.q: In which step of the methodology do you find out whether anything changed on the network recently?
questions.e: Gathering information, questioning users, identifying symptoms and determining recent changes are all part of identifying the problem.

questions.q: Testing has confirmed your theory. What is the next step?
o: Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem and identify potential effects
questions.e: Once you know the cause, plan the fix and think through what it might affect before implementing it.

questions.q: Why document even simple fixes?
o: So others can solve the same problem faster and recurring issues can be spotted
Because the user asks for it
It isn't necessary for simple fixes
questions.e: Documentation builds a knowledge base and shows trends that point to underlying problems.

questions.q: A user says their PC has no network connection. Which is a 'question the obvious' check?
o: Is the network cable plugged in and is the link light on?
Is the core router's firmware up to date?
Is the DNS server's PTR record correct?
questions.e: Simple physical causes are common and quick to rule out.

questions.q: A technician suspects a faulty switch port, moves the PC to another port and it works. Which step was this?
o: Test the theory to determine the cause
questions.e: Moving the PC confirms (or rules out) the theory that the port is at fault.

questions.q: What should a plan of action consider before it's put in place?
o: Potential effects, such as downtime, other users affected and the need for change approval
What the user would like the answer to be
questions.e: A fix that causes a wider outage is worse than the original problem.

questions.q: The fix needs a firewall change the technician isn't allowed to make. What should they do?
o: Escalate to the team that owns the firewall
Tell the user nothing can be done
questions.e: The 'implement the solution or escalate as necessary' step covers handing over to the right people.

questions.q: Why change only one thing at a time when testing a theory?
o: So you know which change fixed the problem, and can undo it if it didn't
questions.e: Changing several things at once makes it impossible to know what worked and harder to reverse.

questions.q: A loop was caused by a user plugging a small switch into two wall ports. The loop is cleared. Which preventive measure fits the 'verify and prevent' step?
o: Enable BPDU guard on access ports
questions.e: BPDU guard shuts a user-facing port if it receives spanning tree messages, stopping the problem happening again.

questions.q: A user can reach most websites but not one particular web application. Which approach would you most likely start with?
o: Top-to-bottom, starting at the application layer
questions.e: Since other sites work, the lower layers are probably fine, so starting at the top is quicker.

questions.q: A theory is tested and turns out to be wrong. What should the technician do?
o: Establish a new theory or escalate
questions.e: If testing doesn't confirm the cause, go back and form another theory, or escalate if you've run out of ideas.

questions.q: Which PoE standard supplies up to about 15.4 W per port?
questions.e: 802.3af is PoE (15.4 W), 802.3at is PoE+ (30 W) and 802.3bt is PoE++ (60 W or more). 802.3ad is link aggregation.

questions.q: Which PoE standard can supply 60 W or more per port, for devices such as PTZ cameras and some access points?
questions.e: 802.3bt Type 3 provides up to 60 W and Type 4 up to 90 W at the switch.

questions.q: A cable tester shows pairs 1-2 and 3-6 crossed at one end of a cable meant to be straight-through. What is the fault?
o: Incorrect termination, as one end is wired to the wrong pinout
questions.e: Both ends of a straight-through cable should use the same standard, usually T568B. Re-terminate the wrong end.

questions.q: An interface shows a large number of late collisions. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Late collisions happen when one side is half duplex and the other full duplex. Set both ends to auto, or both to the same settings.

questions.q: A new camera needs PoE+, but the switch only supports 802.3af. What is likely to happen?
o: The camera may not power up, or may run with features such as heating or zoom disabled
The switch upgrades itself to PoE+
The camera draws power from the network cable's data pairs only
questions.e: Devices that need more power than the port can give will fail or fall back to a limited mode.

questions.q: Why can shielded twisted pair cause problems if it isn't grounded properly?
o: The shield can pick up noise and act like an antenna instead of blocking interference
It makes the cable too short
It turns the cable into fibre
questions.e: STP only works as intended when the shield is bonded to earth through the connectors and patch panel.

questions.q: A PC's address is 192.168.1.45/24, but its default gateway is set to 192.168.2.1. What will happen?
o: It can reach local hosts but nothing on other networks
It can't reach anything, even local hosts
It will get an APIPA address
questions.e: The gateway must be on the PC's own subnet. Local traffic doesn't use the gateway, so that still works.

questions.q: Which STP port role forwards traffic onto a network segment, one per segment?
questions.e: Each segment has one designated port. Each non-root switch has one root port, its best path towards the root bridge.

questions.q: Users at a branch get 'destination unreachable' when trying to reach a new subnet at head office. The branch router's table has no route to it. What is the fix?
o: Add a route to the new subnet, or make sure the routing protocol advertises it
questions.e: Routers drop traffic for networks they don't know about, unless there's a default route that covers them.

questions.q: Why can a wrong subnet mask let a PC reach some remote hosts but not others?
o: The PC treats some remote addresses as local and tries to reach them directly instead of using the gateway
It changes the PC's MAC address
questions.e: With a mask that's too wide, the PC ARPs for addresses it thinks are on its own network, gets no reply and the traffic fails.

questions.q: What is network contention?
o: Many devices competing for the same bandwidth or medium at the same time
Two routers with the same name
questions.e: Contention is common on shared links and busy Wi-Fi, and shows up as slow speeds at busy times.

questions.q: A continuous ping shows a 'Request timed out' every few replies. What does this show?
questions.e: Each timeout is a lost echo request or reply. Even a few percent of loss hurts voice and video.

questions.q: What is the usual target for one-way latency on VoIP calls?
questions.e: Above about 150 ms one way, people start talking over each other. Jitter and packet loss matter too.

questions.q: Which tool shows whether neighbouring access points are using overlapping channels?
questions.e: A Wi-Fi analyser lists nearby networks, their channels and signal strengths.

questions.q: What does a jitter buffer on a VoIP phone do?
o: Holds incoming packets briefly so they can be played out evenly, at the cost of a little extra delay
questions.e: It smooths out variation in arrival times. If jitter is greater than the buffer can cover, audio still breaks up.

questions.q: Why can adding more access points at full power make Wi-Fi worse?
o: They interfere with each other on shared channels and can keep clients stuck to distant APs
More APs always mean less coverage
APs at full power use less bandwidth
questions.e: Good designs use the right number of APs with power and channels planned, not just more APs.

questions.q: A laptop stays connected to a distant AP with a weak signal even though a closer AP is available. What is this usually called?
o: A sticky client, a roaming problem
questions.e: Clients decide when to roam. Lowering AP power, setting a minimum signal level or enabling roaming assistance features can help.

questions.q: A 100 Mbps link tests at about 90 Mbps. Why isn't that necessarily a fault?
o: Protocol overhead and other traffic mean throughput is always less than the link's bandwidth
Speed tests double the real figure
questions.e: Bandwidth is the theoretical maximum. Throughput is what actually gets through.

questions.q: Which is a common cause of packet loss?
o: Congested queues dropping packets, faulty cables or wireless interference
questions.e: Interface counters, monitoring tools and tests such as ping and traceroute help narrow down where loss happens.

questions.q: Which measurement helps you plan a link upgrade before it becomes a bottleneck?
o: The link's utilisation trend over time compared with its capacity
questions.e: If peak utilisation keeps rising towards 100%, plan the upgrade before users feel it.

questions.q: A traceroute shows about 10 ms for the first few hops, then 180 ms from one hop onwards. What does this suggest?
o: The link into that hop adds the delay, perhaps a long-distance or congested link
questions.e: The jump that carries on through later hops points to that link. A single slow hop that drops back down again is often just a router slow to answer ICMP.

questions.q: What does iPerf measure?
o: The throughput between two hosts, by sending test traffic from a client to a server
questions.e: iPerf is a software speed tester you run on both ends, useful for checking a link's real capacity.

questions.q: Which Windows command shows the MAC address of each network adapter, along with DNS servers and DHCP details?
questions.e: Plain ipconfig shows the basics. Add /all for MAC addresses, DHCP server, lease times and DNS servers.
